title: st.bind() to attach query_params to session state
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

J. Carroll (before he left his position on the team) and I were discussing possible implementations of a new way to integrate `st.query_params` and `st.session_state` on Discord back in March. I am writing this proposal to officially document the idea and see if there's anyone on the Streamlit team who would be willing to "greenlight" this feature or give me a sense of whether it would be welcome.

At it's core, `st.bind()` is a way to declare certain elements of `st.session_state` (including widget values) permanently bound to a corresponding value in `st.query_params` (and by extension, the browser's URL). A basic example of `st.bind()` looks like this:

```python
import streamlit as st

st.bind("user_text")

user_text = st.text_input("Show me what you got", key="user_text", value="rhythm")

st.write("You got", user_text)
```

If you navigate to this page at http://localhost:8501/, you will see 
```
Show me what you got: [  rhythm      ]
You got rhythm
```
and the URL will be updated to http://localhost:8501/?user_text=rhythm

If you navigate to this page at http://localhost:8501/?user_text=music, you will see 
```
Show me what you got: [  music      ]
You got music
```

Any changes to the value of the `text_input` widget are immediately reflected in the page URL.

### Why?

This makes it extremely easy to create "stateful" apps that can be shared with people. Have a dashboard that shows you popularity of different music genres by country and year? With `st.bind()` you can reflect the user inputs for `year` and `genre` into the URL, and then send that URL to someone else so they can pull up the dashboard in the exact same state:

* https://popmusicmap.streamlit.app/?year=2010&genre=funk
* https://popmusicmap.streamlit.app/?year=2012&genre=R%26B&genre=country&genre=gospel

```python
import streamlit as st
from my_app import music_popularity_map, genre_options

st.bind(["year", "genre"])

year = st.number_input("Pick a year", key="year", min_value=2000, max_value=2023)
genres = st.multiselect("Pick some genres", key="genre" options=genre_options)

music_popularity_map(year, genres)
```

What does this feature offer over just using `st.query_params`? It avoids a lot of boilerplate and conversion code, for one. To do this without `st.bind` would require a lot of legwork:

```python
import streamlit as st
from my_app import music_popularity_map, genre_options

year_string_from_url = st.query_params.get("year", "2000")
try:
     st.session_state.year = int(year_string_from_url)
except ValueError:
     pass

def update_year_callback():
    if "year" in st.session_state:
        st.query_params.year = str(st.session_state.year)

year = st.number_input("Pick a year", key="year", min_value=2000, max_value=2023, on_change=update_year_callback)
genres = st.multiselect("Pick some genres", key="genre" options=genre_options)

music_popularity_map(year, genres)
````
And all that for just ONE widget!

My own extension's demo, https://query-string.streamlit.app/, has some other examples of the kinds of things you can do with this kind of feature. Due to not having access to all of the streamlit session state internals, it is limited to a smaller selection of widgets and tends to be a bit finicky with some of the more complex widgets like `datetime` or `slider`.

I think an officially supported version of this would benefit a lot of people who are building apps with streamlit.

### How?

`st.bind()` can be implemented as an exposed method of `SafeSessionStateProxy -> SafeSessionState -> SessionState`, which already has access to both `query_params` and `session_state`.

Calling `st.bind("foo")` places a new `BindRegistration` into a datastructure within `SessionState`:
```python
_bind_registry = {
   "foo": BindRegistration("foo", serde=None, deserde=None, plural=None),
   ...
}
```
Values are deserialized into `st.session_state` lazily, meaning a call to `st.session_state.get(key)` will check to see if there is a `BindRegistration` for `key` and will deserialize and return the value without it ever needing to go into any of the existing `SessionState` storage dictionaries.

Because all query params are strings, widgets will supply additional "hints" when calling `register_widget` about what type of object they would like to receive back. If the user did not call `st.bind("foo")` with any additional arguments, then a `st.text_input(key="foo")` will receive `st.query_params.foo` as a string when it registers itself, while a `st.number_input(key="foo", value=0)` would suggest that it wants an integer, and `register_widget` would attempt to deserialize `st.query_params.foo` to an integer.

When a script re-run is triggered, any keyed widgets whose value changed and whose key has a corresponding `BindRegistration` are re-serialized and pushed to the frontend to be updated in the browsers URL bar. This behavior will be made even more seamless once https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/9049 is incorporated, as the app will be able to send these new parameters along with other `NewSession` data at the start of the Rerun, instead of having to rely on a separate `PageInfoChanged` message.

Users could also have the capability to express their own serialization and deserialization methods for each `st.bind()` call, allowing for advanced extensibility of the behavior. 


### Additional Context

If anyone is willing to play coordinator on this feature, I'm more than happy to work on it with the Streamlit team on whatever timeline they feel is appropriate.

title: st.dialog Does Not Close Immediately After User Action if Followed by Blocking Operation (e.g. time.sleep(15))
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

When using `st.dialog` to collect feedback from a user, if the feedback submission is followed by a blocking operation (e.g., `time.sleep(15)`), the dialog's title remains visible on the screen until the blocking operation is complete. This creates a poor user experience because the user may expect the dialog to disappear immediately after submitting their input, but the dialog remains visible until the blocking operation finishes.


### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import time
import streamlit as st

@st.dialog("Cast your vote")
def vote(item):
    st.write(f"Why is {item} your favorite?")
    reason = st.text_input("Because...")
    if st.button("Submit"):
        st.session_state.vote = {"item": item, "reason": reason}
        st.rerun()

if "vote" not in st.session_state:
    st.write("Vote for your favorite")

    if st.button("A"):
        vote("A")
    if st.button("B"):
        vote("B")
else:
    time.sleep(15)
    f"You voted for {st.session_state.vote['item']} because {st.session_state.vote['reason']}"
```


### Steps To Reproduce

1. Use the provided code below to mimic collecting user feedback using `st.dialog`.
2. After the user submits their feedback, the code simulates a blocking operation using `time.sleep(15)`.
3. Notice that the dialog's title ("Cast your vote") remains visible for the full 15 seconds while `time.sleep(15)` is running.

### Expected Behavior

The dialog should close immediately after the user submits their input, regardless of any blocking operation that follows, so that the UI responds promptly to the user's action.

### Current Behavior

The dialog remains open until the blocking operation (`time.sleep(15)`) is completed. This means the title "Cast your vote" is displayed on the screen for 15 seconds.

![2024-09-04_21-39-12 (1)](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f664f9f7-24cf-4b3b-8fad-d5fdcf0dcfdb)


### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.37.1
- Python version: 3.9
- Operating System: Mac OS / Linux Ubuntu 
- Browser: Chrome 


### Additional Information

### GIF:
_Attach a GIF that shows the issue occurring._

### Additional Context:

I plan to use `st.dialog` to collect user confirmation before running a long operation. However, due to this behavior, the dialog title remains visible until the operation completes, making the user experience confusing. Ideally, the dialog should close immediately after the user interaction, regardless of subsequent operations.

title: Exponential slowdown in Streamlit as the number of widgets increases (starting in v1.34)
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

There is an exponential slowdown in Streamlit as the number of input widgets is increases. This started happening with the 1.34 release and is tied to PR #8529. Calling [`get_session_state()`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/number_input.py#L390) in the widgets is triggering this [dict comp method](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/lib/streamlit/runtime/state/session_state.py#L370) exponentially more times than previously. For a simple app containing 200 number inputs, there is a 50x increase in calls to `_reverse_key_wid_map` which causes the app to take over 1s to re-load locally (vs ~0.2s with release 1.33). Here is a plot of the number of calls vs the number of inputs:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4b0ef9c9-49c4-482b-85d9-9684e41f523d)

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st
import time
import random

NUM_TABS = 10
NUM_INPUTS = 20


def create_inputs(t):
    for i in range(NUM_INPUTS):
        key = f"tab_{t + 1}_input_{i + 1}_value"
        if key in st.session_state:
            value = st.session_state[key]
        else:
            value = random.randint(0, 100000)
        st.number_input(
            label=f"Number Input {i + 1}",
            value=value,
            min_value=0,
            step=1,
            format="%d",
            key=key,
        )


def main():
    st.title("My dummy app")
    with st.container(border=True, height=500):
        tabs = st.tabs([f"Tab {i + 1}" for i in range(NUM_TABS)])
        for t, tab in enumerate(tabs):
            with tab:
                create_inputs(t)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import cProfile
    from pstats import Stats

    pr = cProfile.Profile()
    pr.enable()

    start_time = time.time()
    main()
    st.info(f"run time: {time.time() - start_time:.3f} seconds")

    pr.disable()
    stats = Stats(pr)
    stats.sort_stats("tottime").print_stats(10)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app using Streamlit version 1.33
2. Adjust `NUM_TABS` value from 1 to 10 and monitor the `cProfile` output
3. Switch to Streamlit version 1.34 or above
4. Repeat step 2

here is a screenshot of the cProfile output with Streamlit 1.33 using 200 widgets:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2c39e939-5cc9-407a-99f1-e1c9de0257b2)

and here's a screenshot using Streamlit 1.34:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3da40e2d-025c-4752-9a96-6b10b233a0bd)

### Expected Behavior

_No response_

### Current Behavior

_No response_

### Is this a regression?

- [x] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.33 vs 1.34+
- Python version: 3.11
- Operating System: Windows 10
- Browser: Chrome


### Additional Information

_No response_

st.sidebar.button("test_widgets")

    for metric_idx, metric_tab in enumerate(metric_tabs):
        metric = METRICS[metric_idx]
        metric_alias = list(METRIC_ALIASES.values())[metric_idx]

        # Drop-down for category definition

title: `st.container` : Enable horizontal scrolling
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Containers today only enable a vertical scrolling of inner elements (widgets, or nested containers). Enabling horizontal behaviour would allow a lot of new interesting UI/UX patterns to emerge.

### Why?

There has been several occurences where I thought a horizontal container would work best, as a method to optimize the layout for complex ideas. For example, when developing a sort of workbench for a specific AI use case, where I want to build a lot of different purpose driven interfaces.

I feel that some basic but powerful layout options like horizontal scrolling is still what hinders from using streamlit has a SPA/App Platform when the use case gets richer.

### How?

Introduce the `direction` or `scrolling` parameter to `st.container` . I believe containers are the right place for layout options, since they can be nested into columns and combine to create very rich and intuitive horizontal and vertical layout options, without much cognitive load. 

### Additional Context

Today, creating something similar to this requires a lot of column nesting which in my experience is tough to make readable at all screen sizes, and is very annoying to develop for.

title: torch.tensor should play well with st.write
body: ### Checklist - [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue. ### Summary Streamlit has arguable the most beautiful visualization of array data (like Numpy arrays) and tabular data (like Pandas dataframes) of any Python visualization library. All of these visualizations can be effortlessly accessed through the magic of `st.write`. Amazing! However, as data compute moves to GPU-accelerate and distributed environments, new primitives, such as PyTorch tensors are rapidly replacing these older primtives, while have similar visual properties, but are instantly and properly displayed by `st.write` which risks making Streamlit feel dated relative to trends modern AI programming. This GitHub issue covers a minor but obvious first step: rendering `torch.tensor` similarly to how we render `numpy.ndarray`. ### Why? I'd love if `st.write(pytorch_tensor)` felt amazing. ### How? Ideally, the following code which creates a **pytorch** array: ```python torch_array = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3]) st.write(torch_array) ``` Would display identically to this code which creates a **numpy** array: ```python numpy_array = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3]).numpy() st.write(numpy_array) ``` Visually: ### Additional Context This GitHub issue *only* covers the case of `torch.tensor` because 1. Streamlit already beautiful visualization of such objects 2. It is such a basic primitive for writing, understanding, debugging, and presenting GPU-accelerate machine learning code. However, a more ambitious project, would be to wrap all the "natural" PyTorch primitives, potentially covering: - **Tensors** (`torch.tensor`): Multi-dimensional arrays holding data, easily printable in text or graphical form. - **Modules** (`torch.nn.Module`): Defines neural networks, with structures that can be printed or visualized. **Note:** We could potentially use PyTorch's own `torchviz` for this. Or do something extra beautiful in Streamlit. - **Parameters** (`torch.nn.Parameter`): Tensors that are part of the model’s learnable parameters, also printable. - **Datasets** (`torch.utils.data.Dataset`): Contains structured data that can be accessed and printed. - **Data Loaders** (`torch.utils.data.DataLoader`): Provides batches of data for training, easily printable batch-by-batch. - **Gradients** (`torch.Tensor.backward()`): Computes and stores gradients in tensors, which can be printed out. This is obviously a giant project, but it would also ground Streamlit firmly as an AI-centered library for building and exploring large models in the future. :heart:

### Summary

I encountered an issue while trying to pass data between the pages in my multi-page app. After some research, I discovered that setting "showSidebarNavigation = false" in the .streamlit/config.toml file prevents data from being passed between pages. from jupyter_client import KernelManager

title: After first input, st.number_input requires to input twice to get the right value returned if the widget's value parameter is assigned a class property which is stored in st.session_state
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

st.number_input is expected return the increase number by 1 after clicked on +, and keep increasing the value after each click on +. It cannot work as expected if its value parameter is assigned a class property and the class/object which is stored in st.session_state.

After first input, st.number_input requires to input twice to get the right value returned if the widget's value parameter is assigned from a class property.

The same behavior even if keys in the value directly to the widget. Similar behavior is observed on st.text_input, st.date_input,  st.text_area  as well. Maybe more.

### Reproducible Code Example

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-9657)

```Python
import datetime
import streamlit as st

class EES():
    amount: int = 0

if 'ees' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.ees = EES()
    st.session_state.ees.amount = 1
    st.session_state.logs = []

st.write('before', datetime.datetime.now(), st.session_state.ees.amount)

value = st.number_input("Value", min_value=0, value=st.session_state.ees.amount)

if value != st.session_state.ees.amount:
    msg = 'number changed'
    st.write('after', datetime.datetime.now(), value, st.session_state.ees.amount, msg)
    st.session_state.ees.amount = value
    # st.rerun()
else:
    msg = 'no change'

st.session_state.logs.append(str([value, msg]))

st.write('end', datetime.datetime.now(), st.session_state.ees.amount)

st.write('change log', st.session_state.logs)
```


### Steps To Reproduce

1. run the code example
2. click the + of the number input widget for several times

### Expected Behavior

The value should be increased by 1 on each click on the +. The value change log should be as following.

[1, 'no change']
[2, 'number changed']
[3, 'number changed']
[4, 'number changed']
[5, 'number changed']

### Current Behavior

The value change log is as following. Three clicks on + are required in order get it from 1 to 3. It happens the same if keys in the value directly to the widget. Similar behavior is observed on st.text_input as well.

[1, 'no change']
[2, 'number changed']
[2, 'no change']
[3, 'number changed']
[3, 'no change']
[4, 'number changed']
[4, 'no change']
[5, 'number changed']

title: Using AppTest, st.dialog does not execute code within st.buttons
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

In previous versions of `streamlit`, I built a confirmation dialog using [streamlit_modal](https://github.com/teamtv/streamlit_modal), which worked fine - also during testing using `streamlit.testing.AppTest`.

Now I transitioned to the new `@st.dialog` decorator, because it feels smoother and is easier to use. But I discovered some strange behavior during testing:  
The code inside the confirmation button, which is inside the dialog, is never executed during testing.

My current understanding is, that the state of the confirmation button is set to `True`, but during the necessary `at.rerun()` the state of the button to show the dialog is reset - therefore the dialog and the button function are not executed again.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

st.session_state.setdefault('confirm', False)

@st.dialog('Confirmation')
def confirmation_dialog():

    if st.button('confirm', key='k_btn_confirm'):
        st.session_state.confirm = True
        st.rerun()

st.write(st.session_state.confirm)

if st.button('Show confirmation dialog', key='k_btn_confirmation_dialog'):
    confirmation_dialog()
```


### Steps To Reproduce

1. Save the code example as `app.py`
2. Start the application using `streamlit run app.py`
3. Observe, that the confirmation dialog works as expected

Now create an additional file `test_dialog.py` with the following content:
```python
from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest


def test_dialog():
    at = AppTest('app.py', default_timeout=30)
    at.run()

    at.button('k_btn_confirmation_dialog').click()
    at.run()

    # at.button('k_btn_confirmation_dialog').click()
    at.button('k_btn_confirm').click()
    at.run()

    assert at.session_state.confirm is True

```

4. Run `pytest` - the final check will fail
5. Include the commented-out line, retriggering the dialog to be shown
6. Re-run `pytest` - the test will now succeed

### Expected Behavior

I would expect `st.dialog` to behave the same way during normal execution and testing.

### Current Behavior

Currently the test fails because the code inside the button `k_btn_confirm` is never executed.

```python
>       assert at.session_state.confirm is True
E       AssertionError: assert False is True

FAILED test_dialog.py::test_dialog - AssertionError: assert False is True
```

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.39.0
- Python version: 3.11.9
- Operating System: Windows 10 Enterprise, Version 22H2, OS build 19045.5011
- Browser: Microsoft Edge for Business, Version 130.0.2849.68 (64-bit)


### Additional Information

My impression is, that this issue is caused by a number of factors playing together:
* `st.rerun()` in button callbacks is a no-op  
requiring you to use the `if st.button(...):` clause
* `AppTest` requires explicit `.run()` calls after widget interaction  
otherwise the fragment would rerun and execute the code within the button
* there is no way to interact with `st.dialog` / `st.fragment` from `AppTest`  
e.g. triggering a rerun of the fragment instead of the whole app

title: Stale output from a long-running computation erroneously shows as not stale when app rerun
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

This is a bug report on behalf of Thiago in order to keep it tracked.

When a Streamlit app with long-running computation is stopped and then re-run, old stale data from the previous run show up as if it was not stale until the old thread completes execution, at which point the data is properly cleaned up.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import platform
import time

import streamlit as st

st.caption(
    f"""
Running with Python {platform.python_version()} and Streamlit {st.__version__}.
"""
)

"""
This is an app!!
"""


def slow_computation(x):
    st.write("Starting slow computation...")
    time.sleep(10)
    st.write("Stopping slow computation...")
    return f"Done, {x + 1}"


out = slow_computation(1)

st.write(out)
```


### Steps To Reproduce

This is a Playwright test that simulates the current behavior (which is to say, this test currently passes, but should fail once the underlying issue is fixed). There are `NOTE`s inline that describe expected behavior


```py
import time

from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect


def test_threading_behavior(page: Page):
    # This uses `localhost:8501` since I was running different versions of Streamlit
    # in an attempt to bisect this issue in case it was introduced at some point in time
    page.goto("http://localhost:8501/")

    page.get_by_text("Stopping slow computation...").wait_for(timeout=20000)
    expect(page.get_by_text("Stopping slow computation...")).to_be_visible()

    print(page.query_selector_all(".element-container")[0].inner_text())

    # At this point, the first run of the thread completed
    expect(page.get_by_text("Done, 2")).to_be_visible()

    # conditional logic to make it work with older versions of Streamlit
    if page.query_selector('div[data-testid="stMainMenu"]'):
        page.get_by_test_id("stMainMenu").click()
    elif page.query_selector('[id="MainMenu"]'):
        main_menu = page.query_selector('[id="MainMenu"]')
        if main_menu:
            main_menu.click()

    # Now we are re-running the app
    page.get_by_text("Rerun").click()

    # Some time delay so that the new thread is started and some elements are marked as stable
    time.sleep(2)

    # Expect some of the elements to be marked as stale
    assert len(page.query_selector_all('div[data-stale="true"]')) == 2
    expect(page.get_by_text("Stopping slow computation...")).to_be_visible()
    expect(page.get_by_text("Done, 2")).to_be_visible()

    # Stop the new thread
    page.get_by_role("button", name="Stop").click()

    time.sleep(2)

    # NOTE: This should not pass. Stale elements shouldn't suddenly be marked as not stale
    # since these are old results from a thread that was supposed to have been stopped
    assert len(page.query_selector_all('div[data-stale="true"]')) == 0

    # NOTE: This should not pass. It is unexpected that the results from the old thread
    # are still showing up, despite us re-running
    expect(page.get_by_text("Stopping slow computation...")).to_be_visible()
    expect(page.get_by_text("Done, 2")).to_be_visible()

    # wait for the thread to complete
    time.sleep(10)

    # Expect old elements to be cleared out
    expect(page.get_by_text("Stopping slow computation...")).not_to_be_visible()
    expect(page.get_by_text("Done, 2")).not_to_be_visible()
```

### Expected Behavior

_No response_

### Current Behavior

_No response_

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.0.0 -> 1.40.1 all show this behavior (I didn't test versions before)
- Python version: 3.8
- Operating System: Mac

title: `st.date_input` doesn't show placeholder text when the initial value is a list of size one
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

You can pass a list to `st.date_input`'s `value` parameter. An empty list will initialize the widget with an empty interval (showing placeholder text). A pair of values will initialize the widget with the given interval (showing the dates as an initial selection). However, if you pass a list of size one, the widget has only the starting date of the interval initialized with no end date. Instead of showing placeholder text for the end date, it's blank.

```
import streamlit as st
from datetime import date, datetime

a = st.selectbox("A", ["today", "2024-10-01", date(2024,9,1), datetime(2024,8,1,12,0,0,0), None])
b = st.selectbox("B", ["today", "2024-10-01", date(2024,9,1), datetime(2024,8,1,12,0,0,0), None])

x = st.date_input("Two-list", [a,b])
x
y = st.date_input("One-list", [a])
y
z = st.date_input("Empty-list", [])
z
```

### Why?

Presumably, it would look better to show placeholder text for the end date when only the initial date of a range is selected. This is also how an intermediate state looks if someone selects a new start date and clicks out of the widget before selecting the end date.

### How?

If someone unfocuses an (interval) date widget with only the start date selected, show the placeholder text for the missing end date.

title: More consistent handling of relative paths
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

We have two main ways relative paths are parsed:
- For Page and navigation commands, paths are relative to the entrypoint file
- For most other command (like media), paths are relative to the current working directory

Although this may be the same for many people, Community Cloud in particular used the root of the repository as the current working directory which can necessitate some rearranging of files/path handling for complex apps. When it comes to Community Cloud's handling of Python dependencies, both the entrypoint-file directory and the root of the repository are searched, in that order. (This is not the case for packages.txt, nor for Streamlit's config.toml. The former must be handled in Cloud, but the latter may be handled in open source.)

It would be nice if all of Streamlit's paths prioritized "relative to the entrypoint file" then fell back to "relative to the current working directory." This could be implemented for `.streamlit/config.toml` (or anything in the `.streamlit` folder before falling back to the user's global settings). This could also be used for all local file paths (`st.image`, `st.video`, etc).

Related to #7731, #7578 (though more restrictive than those requests).

cc @tvst @sfc-gh-tteixeira 

### Why?

Consistency.

title: Fragment to fragment (co-fragment) communication instead of rerunning entire app
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Would be great to create a functionality for co-fragment communication directly rather than re-running the entire app. This could be streamlit's blockhain moment - no middle men (in this case the entire app).

### Why?

Re-rendering the entire app for co-fragment communication is frustration slow. Co-fragment communication would drastically increase the speed and performance of a streamlit app. 

### How?

My app looks like the below:

![fragments](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f5e0ea57-452c-4696-89c2-112ac27dd9b2)

The black outlines are fragments. The purple/pink outlines are nested fragments. I understand co-fragment communication occurs through session_state which is great but for this communication to be recognised, one must re-run the whole app. This makes the app more slow and somewhat buggy in my experience of operating my app. 

Seeing as fragments can be re-run periodically, it would be great to add the possibility to communicate between specific fragments via an action. For example, in my app image, After I input details in the "Contact Details" expander, I want to update the CV Preview fragment. But to do that, I have to re-run the entire app. Perhaps the possibility to rerun specific fragments based on some unique Id (like a key of a streamlit widget) when I say click on the submit form button in the Contact Details expander would be great. 

Just an example
```
@st.fragment(key="test_frag", keys_to_update=["frag1", "frag2"])
```

The issue with the above is for every rerun action, the `keys to update` will rerun. So perhaps, we could create a trigger command parameter.

```
@st.fragment(key="test_frag", keys_to_update=["frag1", "frag2"], trigger_keys=["form_submit_btn"])
```

We could also get fancy and connect trigger keys to keys to update:


```
@st.fragment(key="test_frag", keys_to_update=["frag1", "frag2"], trigger_keys=[{"frag1":"form_submit_btn"}])
```

title: `st.server_state` with endpoint access (like `st.session_state`, but for global values; different from pickled user sessions)
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Currently, we can use `st.cache_data` and `st.cache_resource` to "save" values that can be accessed between sessions. What if there was an API similar to `st.session_state` that was shared between sessions? I suggest `st.server_state`.

Additionally, a Streamlit app could include an endpoint for accessing and updating server state.

### Why?

A common pattern is for a Streamlit app to reach out and collect data from a remote location, typically saving it with `st.cache_data`. If there was some server state combined with an endpoint, a remote source could be able to ping the app and initiate an update of data. This prevents needing to schedule an app to run to update data or making a random user wait if they are the first to connect beyond a cached values TTL.

This would also be useful for IoT use cases where a smart device can send an alert to the app.

Another feature request to send a global message to all sessions (#7312) could also be accommodated with this.

### How?

Add a new API `st.server_state` which is global with all sessions having read/write access.
Add an (authenticated) enpoint for remote sources to connect to and update values in `st.server_state`.

### Additional Context

This is related to requests for app state (#8609), but I'm suggesting something narrower.

title: Session State convenience function for initialization
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

It'd be nice for Session State to have a convenience method for initializing it.

### Why?

Many apps have boilerplate code:
```python
if "my_key" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.my_key = "default_value"
```
If there are multiple keys, you might shortcut the logical test to check for one and initialize all others:
```python
if "A" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.A = "A"
    st.session_state.B = "B"
    st.session_state.C = "C"
```
If any of the keys were associated to a widget and the widget wasn't continuously rendered, you could have a situation will all keys initialized on session start, but maybe "B" or "C" got deleted later. Thus, to be really thorough, you'd need:

```python
session_init = {"A":"A", "B":"B", "C":"C"}
for key, value in session_init.items():
    st.session_state[key] = value
```

It might be nice to have a convenience function to handle the latter:

```python
st.session_state.from_dict({"A":"A", "B":"B", "C":"C"})
```

A parameter could be used to distinguish between initializing (set if not exists), updating (dictionary merge), or full replacement (delete other keys).


### How?

Similar to how `st.query_params` is a dict-like interface with a few extra functions, `st.session_state` could get a convenience function or two.

### Additional Context

title: Support Multi-Tenant Folder Structure for Built-In Pages Navigation
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Currently, Streamlit automatically generates a sidebar navigation based on the scripts in a pages/ folder. I’d like to extend this to support tenant-based folders, so that each authenticated user (tenant) sees only the pages within their designated folder. This would enable a seamless multi-tenant dashboard structure within a single Streamlit app.

### Why?

1. Multi-Tenant Support: In many SaaS scenarios, each tenant (or client/project) has unique pages or dashboards.
2. Scalability: Storing tenant-specific pages in dedicated folders would keep the codebase organized, while reusing common components across tenants.
3. Security & Personalization: Automatically generating the correct sidebar for each tenant ensures that users only see content relevant to their role or tenant.

### How?

- Extended Pages Folder: Introduce an optional directory structure such as:
        tenants/
          --tenant1/
            ----page1.py
            ---- page2.py
          --tenant2/
            ----page1.py
            ----page2.py
- Automatic Side Nav: Streamlit would detect these sub-folders at runtime (similar to how it currently handles pages/) and generate a tenant-specific navigation based on authentication or session state.
- Role/Tenant Check: When a user logs in, Streamlit could read a tenant or role from st.session_state and render pages from the corresponding tenant folder only.
- Optional Config: Perhaps a parameter or config setting in config.toml (e.g., multi_tenant = true) that, when enabled, triggers this multi-folder scanning and nav generation.

title: on_change callback is triggered without user-interaction on in-script delays
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

My end-users noticed that checkboxes were very incidentally being automatically checked or inverted from their initial state. 
Further investigation showed that some checkboxes their `on_change` callbacks are triggered without user-interaction.

title: Expose OAuth errors during `st.login`
body:
### Checklist

- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

We're soon launching native authentication in Streamlit (see #8518). One thing we left out for now is handling errors that appear during the OAuth flow. It would be great to either handle them automatically (e.g. by showing a dialog or toast) or exposing them programmatically. 


### Why?

These errors should be very rare in Streamlit because many errors are handled directly in the OAuth flow by the identity provider and [most possible errors that are propagated back to the app](https://www.oauth.com/oauth2-servers/server-side-apps/possible-errors/) are due to a) wrong configuration (which we usually catch before even initiating the OAuth flow), b) wrong implementation (which we control), or c) the server of the identity provider being down (which shouldn't happen often for the major providers). 

But errors can still happen – the most prominent example we found during testing is when the user clicks "Cancel" on the consent screen shown when logging in for the first time. And there might be others we didn't think about yet. 

### How?

Two possible ways:

1. Automatically show a dialog or toast with the error code and potentially error description and error URI. Note that OAuth recommends showing a custom error message to the user instead of showing the error code and error description directly. But I think in our case (where these errors are very rare), it might be fine to just show that and not require the developer to implement it themselves. We should probably have a parameter on `st.login` to disable this automatic notification in case the developer wants to handle the error themselves (see 2). 
2. Expose the error details programmatically. One way would be to put it into `st.user` as keys `error`, `error_description` (optional), and `error_uri` (optional). In that case, we should automatically clear these items on the next rerun, otherwise it becomes very hard to only show the error when it happens. Another possible approach would be to have an `on_error` callback on `st.login`. But a) we'd need to pass the error details to this callback, which would make it work a bit differently than our callbacks (currently) work and b) it's a bit more cumbersome to work with this in practice because you often have to stick the error message into `st.session_state` if you want to show it somewhere within the app. 

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: Pending changes to a widget are not submitted if interrupted by `st.rerun()` or `st.switch_page()`.
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

This might not be a bug exactly, but the consequence is that it can result in a seemingly invalid state. Hence, I'll mark this as a bug.

Background: If there is a pending edit in some widget like `st.text_area` and a user clicks a button, Streamlit will process the widget's new value and any associated callback immediately before the button's and then proceed with the rerun.

In contrast: If a pending edit exists for a widget and the app is programmatically rerun (`st.rerun()`, `st.switch_page`), then the edit is preserved on the frontend, but not submitted to the backend. This can result in the front end appearing to have a different value than the back end.


### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st
import time

if "disabled" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.disabled = False

x = st.text_area("Test", key="test", disabled=st.session_state.disabled)

st.session_state

if st.session_state.disabled == False:
    st.write("Running")
    time.sleep(3)
    st.session_state.disabled = True
    st.rerun()

if st.button("Reset"):
    st.session_state.disabled = False
    st.rerun()

st.session_state
```


### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app
2. Type something into the text area within three seconds, but don't click out.
3. The app will rerun and make the widget disabled.

The front end will have the pending value but the output will remain as the default value.

4. Click "Reset"

The widget will be reenabled and focus will return to it, but if you do nothing the app will rerun again again and disable the widget, still with the mismatch between front end and back end.

### Expected Behavior

The front end and back end should not disagree on a widget's value, especially through multiple reruns.

### Current Behavior

A disabled widget appears to have one value on the front end, but has a different value on the back end.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.41.1
- Python version: 3.11.8
- Operating System: macOS
- Browser: Chrome


### Additional Information

If I create two widgets that time out in succession, then upon re-enabling them, they will both be in focus simultaneously with their pending edits. In general, a user can proceed to interact with the rest of the app and these odd-state elements will remain focused until the user clicks into and out of them to submit the pending value. Hence, maybe not a bug exactly, but it looks convincingly "wrong" in the disabled state and it's certainly strange UI for multiple widgets to be focused at the same time.

title: Rerun fragment from anywhere, not just from within itself
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Related to #8511 and #10045.

Currently the only way to rerun a fragment is calling `st.rerun(scope="fragment")` from within itself. Allowing a fragment rerun to be triggered from anywhere (another fragment or the main app) would unlock new powerful use-cases.  

### Why?

When a fragment is dependent on another fragment or on a change on the main app, the only current way to reflect that dependency is to rerun the full application whenever a dependency changes.

### How?

I think adding a key to each fragment would allow the user to build his custom logic to manage the dependency chain and take full control on when to run a given fragment:

```python
@st.fragment(key="depends_on_b")
def a():
    st.write(st.session_state.input_for_a)

@st.fragment(key="depends_on_main")
def b():
    st.session_state.input_for_a = ...
    if st.button("Should rerun a"):
        st.rerun(scope="fragment", key="depends_on_b")

if other_condition:
    st.rerun(scope="fragment", key="depends_on_main")
```

This implementation doesn't go the full mile to describe the dependency chain in the fragment's definition and let streamlit handle the rerun logic as suggested in #10045, but provides more flexibility for the user to rerun a fragment from anywhere and under any conditions that fits his use-case

### Additional Context

### Summary

Implement support for alert blocks (aka admonitions) within the Streamlit markdown flavour. 

### Why?

This is supported by many other markdown flavours as well.

### How?

Unfortunately, there isn't one common syntax for this... we probably have to choose between one of these:

[Github markdown](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/basic-writing-and-formatting-syntax):

> [!NOTE]  
> This is a note alert block

```
> [!NOTE]  
> This is a note alert block
```

[PyMdown](https://facelessuser.github.io/pymdown-extensions/extensions/details/):

```
??? note
   This is a note alert block
```

[Material for Mkdocs](https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/reference/admonitions/) & [Python Markdown](https://python-markdown.github.io/extensions/admonition/):

```
!!! note

    This is a note alert block
```

[Docusaurus](https://docusaurus.io/docs/markdown-features/admonitions):

```
:::note

This is a note alert block

:::
```

### Additional Context

title: Widget state is not persisted after adding run_every to a fragment
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

To persist widget values I use the interrupt the widget clean-up process documented [here](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/widget-behavior#interrupting-the-widget-clean-up-process).
I find this works very well for me, until recently, when I added a fragment with `run_every=2`, and now I notice that the session state is not persisting between pages.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import streamlit as st

key = "test_radio"
options = ["option 1", "option 2"]
print(f"State value for {key} is {st.session_state.get(key, 'unset')}")
st.session_state[key] = st.session_state.get(key, options[0]) # Interrupt cleanup, and set a default value for the key
st.radio("Test radio", options=options, key=key)

@st.fragment(run_every=2)
def test_fragment():
    pass

test_fragment() # Commenting this changes the behaviour
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Create `main.py` and `pages/1_other_page.py` with the code from "Reproducible Code Example"
2. Launch the app and choose "option 2".
3. Wait 2 seconds then navigate to "Other Page".
4. Observe "option 1" is selected.
5. Choose "option 2" then immediately navigate back to main page, in under 2 seconds
6. Observe "option 2" is selected.

=== Successful variants ===
A. Comment out the `test_fragment()` line and repeat the test. This time you'll observe "option 2" is always selected, as expected.
B. Remove the `run_every` parameter and repeat the test. This time you'll observe "option 2" is always selected, as expected.

### Expected Behavior

The state values associated with widgets should be available at the top of a new page, before streamlit cleanup process begins. In the given example, "option 2" should stay selected when switching between pages.

### Current Behavior

Widget state is being cleared out prematurely.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Python version: 3.10.14

body:
### Checklist

### Summary

When formatting cells of a dataframe using pandas styler and rendering it via the `st.data_editor` the performance can be decreased significantly, especially for dataframes with several hundred rows and tens of columns (see example in Additional Context section). The recording is from a Macbook Pro with M2 processor, on other laptops the performance is even worse (showing the same dataframe without formatting/styling works well though).
A more performant way of formatting/styling dataframes shown via `st.data_editor` or `st.dataframe` would improve user experience drastically.

### Why?

`st.data_editor`and `st.dataframe` are hardly usable, especially on entry and mid-level laptops, when styling the dataframe.
A more performant styling would be great.
In our case, we want to use background color formatting for columns that are not editable, to make it easy to spot for the users, which columns they can edit.

### How?

If the degradation in performance is linked to the usage of pandas styler (mentioned in this issue: https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/6340), a new styling process would have to be developed that ensures good rendering performance also for dataframes with hundreds of rows and tens of columns.

### Additional Context

Code example and demo video:

body: ### Checklist - [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue. ### Summary Currently `st.data_editor` allows for formatting/styling non-editable "disabled" columns via pandas styler (see sample code and screenshot in Additional Context section). However, editable columns cannot be formatted, especially background and font color. It would be great to have conditional formatting/styling options on editable columns as well. Additionally, the currently available formatting options for numeric data are still limited [st.column_config.NumberColumn](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/data/st.column_config/st.column_config.numbercolumn) Support for bold font would be amazing, too. ### Why? In my current use case, I added Sub/Total rows into a table with some editable and non-editable columns. These Sub/Total columns should have a background color to be highlighted from the other rows containing raw data. Currently, only non-editable columns get the background color applied. Additionally, the currently available formatting options for numeric data are limited. An option to have "," seperator for thousands but no decimals is not available (only with 2 decimals via `format="accounting"` of `st.column_config.NumberColumn`). It would also be great to have conditional formatting to highlight new user input or specific values in editable columns. ### How? This could be implemented like for non-editable "disabled" columns, so via pandas Styler. Other (more performant) styling options would also be great. ### Additional Context Related issues touching on extended styling options in `st.data_editor`: #6340 and #8268 Sample code and screenshot (python 3.11, streamlit 1.44): "Column 16" is the only editable column and should be formatted exactly like "Column 15" (yellow bg, red font, bold font (not supported atm)) ```python import streamlit as st import pandas as pd import numpy as np st.set_page_config( layout="wide" ) data = 2000*np.random.rand(1000, 30) columns = [f'Column {i+1}' for i in range(30)] df = pd.DataFrame(data, columns=columns) def style_columns(col): return [f'background-color: grey' for _ in col] def font_color(col: pd.Series) -> list[str]: return [f'color:orange' for _ in col] def fully_style_columns(col: pd.Series) -> list[str]: return [f'color:red; font-weight: bold; background-color: yellow' for _ in col] def df_on_change(): st.toast("Edited a cell!") fully_styled_df = (df.style.apply(style_columns, subset=['Column 15']) .apply(fully_style_columns, subset=[f'Column {i+1}' for i in range(14,16)]) .format(precision=2,thousands=',',subset=[f'Column {i+1}' for i in range(30)])) fully_styled_df_editor = st.data_editor(fully_styled_df ,use_container_width=True ,num_rows='fixed' ,disabled = [f'Column {i+1}' for i in range(15)] ,column_order = [f'Column {i+1}' for i in range(30)] ,hide_index=True ,key="fully_styled_df_editor" ,on_change=df_on_change ,row_height=20) ```

title: Preserve session state (e.g. in file, database, or localstorage)
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a mechanism to preserve widget state or anything in `st.session_state` across sessions, e.g. by putting it into a local file, or a small database that we run alongside the Streamlit app, or an external database, or localstorage. 

### Why?

The most common use case here is being able to close the tab, come back to it later, and pick up where you left off. Also somewhat related is preserving session state across multiple pages of a multipage app (see #5813), even though I think we should find a better solution for this. 

### How?

I think we should look at whether we can find a solution that relates to syncing widget state to query params (see #302) since they basically do the same thing, just storing the values in different places. Maybe something like a parameter on every widget `sync="query_params"|"database"|"localstorage"|...`.

It would also be great to make this extensible, so that experienced devs can configure their own places where the session state should be stored (e.g. an external database). 

### Additional Context

_No response_

body:

### Summary

Add a way to color cells in a dataframe without using Pandas Styler. 

### Why?

See some examples of use cases [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/0.17.1/style.html). Users can do this today by using Pandas Styler but that results in slow performance and other disadvantages. We should have a built-in way to do this. 

### How?

Some things we'd probably want:
- Set the color of certain cells specifically (e.g. to highlight important cells).
- Set the color based on the cell value (e.g. different shades of red for negative numbers and green for positive numbers).

Not sure if this should be implemented right in `st.dataframe` or whether we should go through `st.column_config` (which might make more sense since you probably want to have different styling per column).

title: Race condition in Session State Update
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

Updating st.session_state immediately after a UI element interrupts execution flow and causes a race condition, resulting in variables defined in conditional branches being undefined when referenced later.

### Reproducible Code Example

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-11415)

```Python
import streamlit as st

def demo_app():
    st.title("Streamlit Bug Demo")
    
    # Initialize session state
    if 'persistent_choice' not in st.session_state:
        st.session_state.persistent_choice = "Option A"
    
    # Select box with immediate session state update
    options = ["Option A", "Option B"]
    index = 0 if st.session_state.persistent_choice == "Option A" else 1
    choice = st.selectbox("Select an option", options, index=index)
    
    # This line triggers the bug
    st.session_state.persistent_choice = choice
    
    # Variable defined in conditional branches
    result = None
    
    if choice == "Option A":
        st.write("Entering Option A branch")
        result = {"type": "A", "value": 100}
    
    if choice == "Option B":
        st.write("Entering Option B branch")
        result = {"type": "B", "value": 200}
    
    # This line fails with UnboundLocalError
    st.write(f"Result: {result}")

demo_app()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

_No response_

### Expected Behavior

When selecting "Option B", the code should execute the corresponding conditional branch and properly set result.

### Current Behavior

The session state update triggers an immediate rerun, aborting execution before the conditional branches complete. When the script reruns, result remains None and the conditional branches are not entered.

### Checklist


### Summary

The st.file_uploader widget **on mobile phones** exhibits a timeout issue specifically when tested on Android using the Chrome browser. If there is a delay (e.g., around 15 seconds) after opening a file selection application and before selecting a file, the widget fails to upload properly. The issue can be reproduced using the example provided in the official documentation:
[Streamlit File Uploader Documentation](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.file_uploader).

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
# use official demo
# https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.file_uploader

import streamlit as st

uploaded_files = st.file_uploader(
    "Choose a CSV file", accept_multiple_files=True
)
for uploaded_file in uploaded_files:
    bytes_data = uploaded_file.read()
    st.write("filename:", uploaded_file.name)
```

[![Open in Streamlit Cloud](https://static.streamlit.io/badges/streamlit_badge_black_white.svg)](https://issues.streamlitapp.com/?issue=gh-11419)

### Steps To Reproduce

- Open a mobile browser on an Android device (tested with Chrome).
- Visit the official Streamlit documentation for st.file_uploader:
- [URL: https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.file_uploader](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference/widgets/st.file_uploader).
- Scroll down to the example for st.file_uploader.
- On the widget, click the "Browse files" button, which prompts Android to ask which application to use.
- Select any file management app (e.g., Samsung's File Browser) but **wait for 15 seconds** before choosing a file.
- Select a file from the file manager app and confirm.

### Expected Behavior

On mobile phone, after selecting the file in the file manager app, the uploaded file name should appear in the Streamlit app, as expected.

### Current Behavior

- On mobile phone, when waiting 15 seconds before selecting the file, the Streamlit app shows "connecting" after selecting the file and then fails to display the uploaded file name.
- On mobile phone, if a file is selected immediately without delay, the widget works as expected, file name is displayed, and no timeout occurs.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Device: Samsung S24
- OS: Android 15.0
- Browser: Chrome 136.0.7103.125
- Python version: 3.10
- Streamlit Version: 1.45.0
- Internet Connection: Stable WiFi during testing.


### Additional Information

- This issue seems time-sensitive and suggests a possible timeout behavior when Android switches between File Manager App and the Browser.
- No issues observed on desktop browsers with the same testing process.

title: Concurrency issues with `st.data_editor` `on_change` callback: Using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` leads to multiple processing or potential data loss
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

**Issue Description:**

When a user edits cells in the `st.data_editor` object, the `on_change` callback function is triggered. If the user makes additional edits while the `on_change` callback is still running, some edits are processed multiple times (in this case, twice for edits of the first interaction and once for the second interaction) when using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` to process the user edits. This occurs because the callback is threaded, and the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` object still includes the edits from the previous user interaction.

**Additional Issue:**

Attempting to fix this revealed another issue: If the `on_change` callback for a previous call takes longer to execute than the latest call, the Streamlit page reloads before the previous `on_change` callbacks are finished. As a result, not all cells of the `st.data_editor` object are updated, leading to potential loss of user edits. This seems to be fixed by using `threading.Lock()` in the on_change callback function.

**Request:**
I found a solution to this, but would like to know if I just use the `st.data_editor` object and corresponding `on_change` callback in a way that they were not meant to be used (passing/using the `session_state` of the `st.data_editor` in the callback).
-> Is there another method to handle user edits on a dataframe, which ensures that those edits are processed exactly once, so neither multiple times nor never before the Streamlit page or `st.fragment` get reloaded?

### Why?

This is relevant when streaming user edits to a backend database, as potentially user edits are send multiple times to the backend, which causes unnecessary traffic, or edits are lost and not sent to the backend at all.

### How?

Solution (including filtering of the `st.data_editor`'s session state and locking threads during the `on_change` callback):
```python
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import threading
import time

st.set_page_config(layout="wide")

# Initialize session state variables if not already done
if "applied_edits" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["applied_edits"] = {}
if "df" not in st.session_state:
    data = np.zeros((1000, 30))
    columns = [f"Column {i + 1}" for i in range(30)]
    df_init = pd.DataFrame(data, columns=columns)
    totals_row = pd.DataFrame(df_init.sum(axis=0)).T
    st.session_state.df = pd.concat([totals_row, df_init], ignore_index=True)
    st.session_state.df["Totals"] = st.session_state.df.sum(axis=1)
if "call" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["call"] = 0
if "lock" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["lock"] = threading.Lock()


def df_on_change(df):
    with st.session_state["lock"]:
        print(f"on_change call: {st.session_state['call']}")
        # Get a copy of all edited rows in this session
        all_edits = st.session_state["df_editor"]["edited_rows"]
        # Filter out the new edits/changes that were/are not processed in a previous call of the df_on_change function
        edited_rows = {
            row: {
                col: val
                for col, val in changes.items()
                if (row not in st.session_state["applied_edits"])
                or (st.session_state["applied_edits"][row].get(col) != val)
            }
            for row, changes in all_edits.items()
        }
        # Update the record of applied edits so the filter above can be applied in the next call of the df_on_change function once again
        for row, changes in edited_rows.items():
            if not changes:
                continue  # no new changes for this row
            if row not in st.session_state["applied_edits"]:
                st.session_state["applied_edits"][row] = {}
            for col, val in changes.items():
                st.session_state["applied_edits"][row][col] = val

        # Log the filtered edits for debugging
        print(f"session state of data editor: {st.session_state['df_editor']}")
        print(f"New edits to apply: {edited_rows}")
        print(f"Applied edits history: {st.session_state['applied_edits']}")

        # Apply the new changes to the DataFrame
        for row, changes in edited_rows.items():
            for col, val in changes.items():
                print(f"writing value {val} to row {row} and column {col}")
                df.loc[row, col] = val
                # simulate a on_change function that requires a long execution time
                time.sleep(1)

        # Recompute totals row based on all data below it
        df.loc[0] = df.iloc[1:].sum(axis=0)
        df["Totals"] = df.sum(axis=1)

        st.toast("Data updated successfully!")
        st.session_state["call"] += 1


# Use st.data_editor with the on_change callback
st.data_editor(
    st.session_state.df,
    use_container_width=True,
    num_rows="fixed",
    disabled=["Totals"],  # prevent editing the totals row
    column_order=[f"Column {i + 1}" for i in range(30)] + ["Totals"],
    key="df_editor",
    on_change=df_on_change,
    args=[st.session_state.df],
    row_height=20,
)
```

In the demo videos below, the user first adds 9 cells at once and then does single cell changes afterwards (on other cells).

Demo video of the code above (terminal output also shows that each edit/cell is just processed once, which is not the case when not filtering the `st.data_editor`'s session state):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9e924ae7-4cc0-4c96-8029-97c98f872548

Demo video without thread locking:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/aac91a5d-536c-4a44-97c0-1219d80684af

title: Only evaluate/download required columns when using an unevaluated Snowpark/PySpark dataframe in charts
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

If you use an unevaluated Snowpark/PySpark dataframe in `st.bar_chart` etc, we do the following:

1. Restrict the dataframe to the first 1000 rows if it's larger. 
2. Evaluate and download the resulting dataframe by calling `to_pandas`. 
3. Drop all columns except the ones we need, e.g. if `x`, `y`, or `color` are set. 
4. Send that dataframe to the frontend and show it. 

To improve performance, it would be better to switch steps 2 and 3, so that we first drop unnecessary columns and then evaluate the dataframe. Especially for dataframes with lots of columns this could result in a speedup. 

### Why?

Performance.

title: Contribution documentation suggestions
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

I cannot edit the Contribution documentation directly to propose changes, because it is a "wiki" page https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/wiki/Contributing I don't have edit access to instead of living directly in https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md

Here are my suggestions based on my struggles building Streamlit on Ubuntu WSL:

https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/wiki/Contributing#ubuntu should have the additions:

* If you are on Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS or earlier, then you will only have access to libprotoc 3.12.4, which is lower than the minimum required version 3.20. Therefore, you will have to `do-release-upgrade`. *(This one could be edited to have the weasel word "might" instead of "will" if you don't believe very strongly in the validity of the detective work I did months ago.)*

* Make sure you have sudo installed. This comes with Ubuntu by default; but if you somehow lack it, you can become root using `su -` and then install sudo with `apt-get install -y sudo`. *(This one is of questionable usefulness, but for some reason I did need to do this at some point.)*

* If you get an error like `error: failed to remove file [blah blah blah]/streamlit/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/streamlit-1.43.2.dist-info/INSTALLER: Permission denied (os error 13)`, try running `sudo chmod -R 777 .venv` first, and/or prefix your `make` command with `sudo`, eg `sudo make all`. *(This one could be moved to the section that talks about WSL, I suppose, since I don't know if this issue ever arises on native linux (I've only run everything through WSL so I don't know what happens on not-WSL).)*

https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/wiki/Contributing#windows should have the addition:

* WSL2 is more likely than WSL1 to work, as there is (or, at least, has been) a [binary compatibility problem](https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/issues/8151) between nodejs and WSL1.

https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/wiki/Contributing#2-grab-the-code should have the addition:

* For implementation reasons, the absolute filepath of the Streamlit directory must not contain any characters that are specially interpreted by the shell. (The shell in question is almost certainly [Bash](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/bash.html).) *(~~If #11741 and #11742 get fixed then this advice will become obsolete.~~ Edit: unfortunately, this one will not be obsolete until https://github.com/protobufjs/protobuf.js/issues/2081 (a thing with a similar problem, that we depend upon internally) is also fixed, and there is little momentum there. Edit 2026-04-29: that was fixed two days ago, so whenever you get on the current version of that dep special characters are back on the menu...!)*
* **(new)** Independent of the previous warning, there should be a warning: Due to [internal implementation reasons](https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html#resolution-algorithm-specification), the absolute filepath of the Streamlit directory must not contain any backslashes.

### Why?

WSL is not officially supported, but neither is it officially anathema, so I'm happy to share these hard-won tips I discovered. Some of the other info relates to platforms that are officially supported.

### How?

You may copy these all verbatim or change them in any way you like. I release all of that text I wrote into the public domain and also the license of this project. Feel free to close this issue when you've determined you've taken all that you want.

### Additional Context

**Trivia**

These tips mostly come from stuff I discovered while working on https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/10829, which was in turn something I started while trying to start working on a pull request for some other feature that I actually wanted.

title: Create an interface to manage frontend state
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

We have `st.session_state` which allows us to manage widget values. I'm proposing an interface to work with frontend states.


### Why?

We recently introduced a pattern for setting the placeholder text of `st.chat_input`. We used `st.session_state` to do this, but the pattern is very different of other uses because `st.chat_input` is more like a trigger than a stateful widget.

It seems more scalable to have a separate interface for "setting stuff on the frontend but not implicitly sending the information back to the Python server or triggering a rerun."

### How?

`st.frontend_state` would have similar access as `st.session_state`: for example,
* `st.frontend_state.<element_key>.focus()` would be a command to set focus on the frontend.
* `st.frontend_state.<element_key>.state("collapsed")` or `state("expanded")` could be available for the sidebar or expanders. (We set the initial state from the backend, but users are free to expand or collapse these items from the frontend without triggering a rerun.)
* `st.frontend_state.<element_state>.disabled(True)` or `disabled(False)` could be used to disable widgets at the beginning of a run and re-enable them at the end of a run if you want to prevent script run interruptions. (As an auto-protection, any widget that is enabled within the widget command but disabled through frontend state must automatically be re-enabled at the end of a script run if the developer didn't do so themselves.)

The idea of `st.frontend_state` would be to cause state changes that don't themselves cause reruns or otherwise report to the Python backend. (Edgecase: If a use has focus on a widget and a partial edit, then forcing focus elsewhere should technically cause a rerun and submit that partial edit, so app developers would be responsible for using focus appropriately.)

### Additional Context

`st.frontend_state` takes inspiration from both `st.session_state` and `AppTest`. It could be used for two-way communication, but be much less restrictive than Session State. That is, there'd be no problem calling it multiple times. You could "retrieve" the current frontend state multiple times if you wanted to detect if the user had expanded/collapsed something in the middle of a rerun. Unlike states that immediately trigger a rerun and are more rigidly controlled within a script run, the "frontend only" states can be set and retrieved multiple times during a run, in general.

Another example: suppose `st.tabs` gets an `on_change` parameter. `on_change="ignore"` is the default and it operates as it does currently, with the tab selection being a frontend state. If we set `on_change="rerun"` or assign a callable, it becomes a widget. In the first case, you could access or set the current tab through `st.frontend_state` (and not impact the flow of the rerun). In the latter case, the selection is a "value" that must be controlled through `st.session_state`, not `st.frontend_state`.

### Checklist


### Summary

Langchain callback handler fails to get context when the tool call happens in seperate thread.

import streamlit as st
from langchain.agents import create_react_agent
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
from streamlit.external.langchain import StreamlitCallbackHandler

@tool
def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Multiply two numbers."""
    return a * b


agent = create_react_agent(
    model=ChatOpenAI(
        model="gpt-4o",
		temperature=0,
		max_tokens=None,
		timeout=None,
		max_retries=2,
		streaming=True
    ),

)

with st.form(key="form"):
    user_input = st.text_input("Ask your own question")
    submit_clicked = st.form_submit_button("Submit Question")

output_container = st.empty()

if submit_clicked:
    output_container = output_container.container()
    output_container.chat_message("user").write(user_input)
    answer_container = output_container.chat_message("assistant", avatar="🦜")

title: Include all warnings (not just deprecation warnings) in `client.showErrorDetails`
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

`client.showErrorDetails` configures the appears of _deprecation_ warnings and errors. Other warnings display in full.

For example, if `client.showErrorDetails = "none"`, `CachedWidgetWarning` will display with the full stack trace.

### Why?

If someone wants to hide stack traces and information about errors, they most likely want to hide all warnings.

### How?

Include all warning in the setting, not just deprecation warnings.

### Additional Context

https://discuss.streamlit.io/t/showerrordetails-not-working-as-expected/118127

title: State not working as expected, at least for checkboxes
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

In the code below, you can hit the buttons to select and deselect all of the checkboxes, no problem. import streamlit as st

#whatever I did here, it's slightly wrong, because uhh sometimes when the user selects something just now and then clicks a button, the button doesn't override it. title: Automatically reformat in CI on lint failure
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Currently, the CI fails a check if `ruff format --check` fails, thus preventing poorly-formatted code from making it into the codebase, which is good. However, the CI should simply make the reformatting commit for the user. This is almost always desireable. And, in rare cases when it's not desireable, the user can always rollback the automatic commit and manually add the noqa comments they will need, or whatever, so no harm no foul.

### Why?

Dev QoL

### How?

I think mypy achieves this with a "pre-commit" github action, but there are probably a couple ways.

### Additional Context

Here's an example from mypy, for reference https://github.com/python/mypy/pull/19494/commits/7f102209eaab90297b6bbac4066419accc281050

I run afoul of lint rules all the time, because I don't care about code line length at all and just keep typing; so I love it when the reformatter just takes care of it without complaint, according to the preferences of the repo owner. The popular python reformatters I know about (ruff, black) are also 100% safe in the sense of never changing code meaning by reformatting (except for the occasional formatter bug). There may be security implications for hooking up this action, altho' probably not more than hooking up other actions.

title: Regression: Selectbox/Multiselect keyboard focus not activating on mobile (only works in desktop mode)
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

On mobile devices, the keyboard does not activate when tapping into a st.selectbox or st.multiselect. This only works if the browser is set to desktop mode.

This is a regression: prior versions (before ~1.27.0) behaved correctly. In fact, there was a previous bug report for the opposite problem (keyboard focus not closing)  https://github.com/issues/recent?issue=streamlit%7Cstreamlit%7C7513

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

option = st.selectbox(
    "Default email",
    ["[REDACTED_EMAIL]", "[REDACTED_EMAIL]", "[REDACTED_EMAIL]"],
    index=None,
    placeholder="Select a saved email or enter a new one",
    accept_new_options=True,
)

st.write(option)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

Run the script above with streamlit run app.py.

Open the app in a mobile browser (tested on Chrome mobile, Firefox mobile)

Tap into the selectbox.

Notice the keyboard does not activate.

Switch browser to “Desktop site” mode → now the keyboard appears.


### Expected Behavior


When tapping a selectbox/multiselect on mobile, the keyboard should activate to allow text input (without needing desktop mode).


### Current Behavior

The selectbox/multiselect opens but the keyboard does not activate, making text input impossible on mobile unless desktop mode is enabled.

I
