title: Modernize Streamlit's default light and dark themes
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Refresh Streamlit's built-in default light and dark themes to feel more modern and polished out of the box — updated colors, typography, spacing, radii, and component styling — so that apps look great by default without custom theming.

### Why?

The default look is what every new app and most demos ship with, so it strongly shapes the perception of Streamlit. The current defaults feel somewhat dated compared to modern design systems (e.g. shadcn, Tailwind, Tremor, Material 3). A refreshed, cohesive default theme would make apps look more professional immediately, improve the first impression for new users, and reduce how often people reach for custom CSS/themes just to look current.

### How?

Revisit the default theme tokens and component styling for both light and dark modes, for example:

- **Color palette:** refined neutrals/grays, a more modern primary color, and better semantic colors (success/warning/error/info) with good contrast in both modes.
- **Dark mode:** ensure it's a first-class, well-balanced theme (not just an inversion) — proper surface elevations, borders, and contrast.
- **Typography:** modern default font, refined sizes/weights/line-heights and hierarchy.
- **Spacing & shape:** consistent spacing scale and slightly softer, contemporary border radii and borders.
- **Components:** cohesive styling across widgets, containers, dataframes, charts, etc.

Considerations:
- Accessibility: maintain/improve WCAG contrast in both themes.
- Backwards compatibility: this changes the look of existing apps, so consider how to roll it out (e.g. a new theme version/opt-in, migration notes) to avoid surprising users.
- Keep it fully overridable via the existing `[theme]` config.

### Additional Context

- Inspiration: modern design systems like shadcn/ui, Tailwind, Tremor, and Material 3.

title: Add server-side (callable) input validation to `st.text_input`
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Extend the existing `validate` parameter of `st.text_input` to also accept a **callable** for server-side validation, executed on the backend when the value is submitted. When validation fails, the input shows an error state with a message and the value is **not** committed (no rerun). Client-side regex validation (`str` / `(regex, message)` tuple) is already implemented and shipped; this issue tracks the remaining **server-side** part of the approved [product spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2025-12-03-text-input-validation/product-spec.md).

### Why?

Client-side regex validation gives instant feedback but can be bypassed and can't express checks that need backend resources (e.g. database lookups) or must be secure. Server-side callable validation covers those cases — username availability, complex business logic, and security-sensitive validation — without the developer having to manually track/display errors or trigger extra reruns.

### How?

Widen the `validate` type to also accept a callable:

```python
st.text_input(
    ...,
    validate: str | tuple[str, str] | Callable[[str], bool | str] | None = None,
    #                                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ NEW (callable)
)
```

The callable is executed on the backend on submit (Enter/blur/form submit) via a deferred-execution pattern (like `st.download_button` with callable data), without a full rerun. It returns `True` (valid), `False` (generic error), or a `str` (custom error message):

```python
def check_username(value: str) -> bool | str:
    if len(value) < 3:
        return "Username must be at least 3 characters."
    if db.username_exists(value):
        return "Username already taken."
    return True

st.text_input("Username", validate=check_username)
```

Key behaviors (from the spec):
- Runs on commit (blur/Enter/form submit), not on initial render; error state clears as the user types.
- Empty string / `None` bypasses validation (requiredness stays a separate future `required` parameter).
- On success: the deferred commit goes through and triggers the normal rerun / `on_change`. On failure: error state, no rerun.
- While validating: loading spinner, submit disabled, 10s timeout, in-progress validation cancelled if the user edits the value.
- Non-`bool`/`str` return or a raised exception → value rejected with a generic error; exception + traceback logged to the backend console (not sent to the frontend).
- Forms: validation runs on form submit (client-side regex first, then callables); all fields must pass before the single submit rerun.

### Additional Context

- Approved product spec: [`specs/2025-12-03-text-input-validation/product-spec.md`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2025-12-03-text-input-validation/product-spec.md) (client-side portion already shipped; this issue covers the server-side callable).
- Future extensions noted in the spec: server-side callable validation for `st.text_area`, `st.column_config.TextColumn`, `st.number_input`, `st.date_input`, `st.selectbox`, and `st.chat_input`.

title: Allow interactive resizing of `st.columns` via drag-and-drop
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a `resizable: bool = False` parameter to `st.columns` that lets users resize columns by dragging the border between them. When enabled, a border indicator appears on hover between adjacent columns, and dragging adjusts their widths interactively. Resizing is purely client-side and does not trigger a rerun. Specced in [PR #14687](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14687).

### Why?

Column widths in `st.columns` are static today — once set via `spec`, they can't be adjusted without changing code and rerunning. Interactive resizing helps with dashboard customization, data exploration (temporarily expand a column to see more), fine-tuning responsive layouts, and adjusting proportions live during demos/presentations. Current workarounds (layout presets via `st.selectbox`, CSS hacks in custom components, or just accepting fixed layouts) are clunky or fragile.

Related: #5003 (deactivate responsiveness of `st.columns`), #6592 (configurable column responsiveness threshold).

### How?

```python
st.columns(
    spec,
    *,
    gap="small",
    vertical_alignment="top",
    border=False,
    width="stretch",
    resizable=False,  # NEW
)
```

- `resizable=False` (default): current fixed-width behavior, no handles.
- `resizable=True`: drag the border between adjacent columns to resize.

Behavior (from the spec):
- **Hover indicator** + `col-resize` cursor over the resize area; border fades in/out (150ms).
- **Drag** resizes only the two adjacent columns; total row width is preserved (neighbor shrinks as one grows); other columns unchanged.
- **Double-click** the handle resets the adjacent pair to their original `spec` proportions.
- **Minimum width** of 64px prevents collapse; throttled updates for performance.
- **Keyboard**: Arrow Left/Right resize in 10px increments when focused.
- **Accessibility**: handles use `role="separator"`, `aria-orientation="vertical"`, `aria-valuenow/min/max`, and visible focus indicators (WCAG 2.1).
- **Touch**: drag works via touch; indicator shows on touch start.
- **Narrow viewports**: when columns stack (below `theme.breakpoints.columns`, 640px), handles are hidden and reappear when it widens.
- **State**: resized widths persist within the session (React state) and reset on refresh, a `spec`/column-count change, or stack/unstack.

### Alternatives considered (from the spec)

- `resizable: bool` (preferred) vs `resize_mode: Literal["off", "drag"]` — boolean chosen to match the existing `border=True` precedent and the binary nature of the feature; can migrate to an enum later if multiple resize modes are demanded.
- Naming: `resizable` over `adjustable` (too generic) / `flexible` (clashes with flexbox).

### Out of scope (future work)

Persist widths across sessions, snap-to-grid, per-column `min_width`/`max_width`, `on_resize` callback, and named/saveable layout presets.

### Additional Context

- Spec: [PR #14687 — \`[spec] Allow interactive resizing of st.columns\`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14687) (`specs/2026-04-08-resizable-columns/product-spec.md`).

title: is_mem_address_str() fails on uppercase hex addresses, breaking st.write() and st.help() object rendering on Windows
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

`is_mem_address_str()` in `lib/streamlit/string_util.py` matches memory-address reprs with the regex `^\<[a-zA-Z_]+[a-zA-Z0-9<>._ ]* at 0x[0-9a-f]+\>$`. The address group only accepts **lowercase** hex digits. On Windows, CPython formats object addresses with **uppercase** hex (e.g. `<__main__.Foo object at 0x0000027B0C1B1550>`), so the function returns `False` for essentially every real object repr on that platform.

Both callers of this helper then take the wrong branch: `st.write(obj)` stops routing plain objects to the object-help view and prints the raw memory address instead, and `st.help()` renders memory addresses as member values while dropping those members' docstrings.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st


class Foo:
    """A Foo."""

    x = 1

    @property
    def e(self):
        "Property e"
        return 5


st.write(Foo())   # expected: rich object-help view. On Windows: raw memory address as inline code.
st.help(Foo)      # expected: property `e` documented. On Windows: "<property object at 0x...>".
```

Minimal check of the helper itself:

```python
from streamlit.string_util import is_mem_address_str


class Foo:
    pass


print(repr(Foo()))                  # <__main__.Foo object at 0x0000023FFDF98AD0>
print(is_mem_address_str(repr(Foo())))          # False   <-- should be True
print(is_mem_address_str("<foo blarg at 0x15ee6f9a0>"))  # True (lowercase only)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. On Windows, run either snippet above (or just the plain-Python helper check — no browser needed).
2. Observe that `is_mem_address_str` returns `False` for a repr it is explicitly designed to detect.

### Expected Behavior

`is_mem_address_str()` should recognize a CPython memory-address repr regardless of the hex casing produced by the platform's C runtime. Consequently:

- `st.write(obj)` renders the object-help view for an object with no other special handling.
- `st.help(SomeClass)` shows the property's docstring and leaves the value slot empty rather than printing a memory address.

### Current Behavior

On Windows (verified with `AppTest`):

```
markdown elements: ['`<__main__.Foo object at 0x0000027B0C1B1550>`']
help elements    : 0
```

`st.help` on a class with a `@property`:

```
name='e' type='property' value='<property object at 0x000002500A1F3240>' doc=''
```

versus the same class instance, which takes the other code path and is correct:

```
name='e' type='property' value='' doc='Property e'
```

The repository's own tests catch this — they currently fail on Windows for exactly this reason:

- `lib/tests/streamlit/write_test.py::StreamlitWriteTest::test_obj_instance` → `AssertionError: Expected 'help' to be called once. Called 0 times.`
- `lib/tests/streamlit/write_test.py::StreamlitWriteTest::test_repr_html`
- `lib/tests/streamlit/write_test.py::StreamlitWriteTest::test_repr_html_no_html_tags_in_string`
- `lib/tests/streamlit/write_test.py::StreamlitWriteTest::test_repr_html_not_callable`
- `lib/tests/streamlit/elements/help_test.py::StHelpTest::test_class_members` → `assert '<property ob...>' == ''`

They pass on Linux/macOS because glibc's `%p` formatting yields lowercase hex, which is why CI has not caught it.

### Root Cause

`lib/streamlit/string_util.py:250-252`

```python
_OBJ_MEM_ADDRESS: Final = re.compile(
    r"^\<[a-zA-Z_]+[a-zA-Z0-9<>._ ]* at 0x[0-9a-f]+\>$"
)
```

`[0-9a-f]+` cannot match `0000027B0C1B1550`.

### Suggested Fix

Accept both casings, e.g. `[0-9a-fA-F]+` (or add `re.IGNORECASE`).

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `is_mem_address_str()` returns `True` for uppercase-hex reprs such as `<__main__.Foo object at 0x0000027B0C1B1550>`.
- [ ] `st.write(obj)` produces a help element (not a markdown memory address) on Windows.
- [ ] `st.help(SomeClass)` no longer renders `<property object at 0x...>` and preserves property docstrings.
- [ ] A regression test covers an uppercase-hex address string so the behavior is asserted independently of the host platform.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Unknown — the regex appears long-standing.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11
- Browser: n/a (reproduced headlessly via `streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest` and direct function calls)

### Additional Information

The two affected call sites are `lib/streamlit/elements/help.py:482` and `lib/streamlit/elements/write.py:576`.

title: st.slider corrupts min_value/max_value when bounds are reversed, silently producing a wrong range
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

`_slider()` tries to swap reversed bounds with two sequential statements, but the second one reads the variable the first one just overwrote:

```python
# lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/slider.py:1081-1083
# Ensure that min <= value(s) <= max, adjusting the bounds as necessary.
min_value = min(min_value, max_value)
max_value = max(min_value, max_value)   # <-- min_value is already the new (smaller) value
```

After line 1082, `min_value` is `min(a, b)`, so line 1083 evaluates `max(min(a, b), b)`, which is always `b`. The original `min_value` can never become the upper bound, so the intended swap never happens. Depending on what `value` is, this silently produces a wrong range or raises an exception quoting numbers the user never passed.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st

# 1. Bounds silently reinterpreted
st.slider("a", 10, 1)                                  # -> range 1..10, value 10

# 2. Upper bound silently invented from `value`
st.slider("b", min_value=10, max_value=1, value=5)     # -> range 1..5  (max_value=1 is gone)

# 3. Spurious exception quoting numbers the user never passed
st.slider("c", min_value=10, max_value=1, value=1)     # -> StreamlitAPIException
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run any of the three lines above.
2. Compare the resulting slider bounds against the arguments passed.

### Expected Behavior

Either of the following would be self-consistent:

- Reject reversed bounds with a clear error naming the two values the caller actually supplied, the way `st.date_input` already does:
  > The `min_value`, set to 2024-01-02, shouldn't be larger than the `max_value`, set to 2024-01-01.
- Or genuinely swap them, so `st.slider("a", 10, 1)` yields a `1..10` slider — which is what the code comment says it intends.

Today it does neither reliably.

### Current Behavior

Verified with `streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest`:

```
slider(min=10, max=1)            -> min=1.0 max=10.0 value=10
slider(min=10, max=1, value=5)   -> min=1.0 max=5.0  value=5
slider(min=10, max=1, value=1)   -> RAISED: Slider `min_value` must be less than the `max_value`.
                                            The values were 1 and 1.
```

Note case 3: the user passed `10` and `1`, but the error reports "The values were 1 and 1" — both numbers have been overwritten by the faulty normalization. Case 2 is the most damaging, because it silently produces a slider whose upper bound (`5`) was never supplied as a bound at all; it leaked in from `value`.

Isolating just the two lines:

```python
min_value, max_value = 10, 1
min_value = min(min_value, max_value)
max_value = max(min_value, max_value)
print(min_value, max_value)   # 1 1     <-- current behavior

min_value, max_value = 10, 1
min_value, max_value = min(min_value, max_value), max(min_value, max_value)
print(min_value, max_value)   # 1 10    <-- intended
```

The `min_value == max_value` guard at line 1137 then fires on values that are an artifact of this bug rather than of user input, and it only catches the case where the corruption happens to collapse both bounds to the same number — which is why `st.slider("x", 5, 5)` errors while `st.slider("x", 10, 1)` does not.

### Suggested Fix

Assign both bounds simultaneously (or compute the max from the original value):

```python
min_value, max_value = min(min_value, max_value), max(min_value, max_value)
```

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `st.slider("b", min_value=10, max_value=1, value=5)` no longer produces a slider whose upper bound came from `value`.
- [ ] Reversed bounds either swap correctly or raise an error that quotes the values the caller actually passed.
- [ ] Test coverage for reversed `min_value`/`max_value` with `value` below, inside, and above the range.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Unknown.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11 (logic is platform-independent)
- Browser: n/a (reproduced headlessly via `streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest`)

### Additional Information

Related but distinct: #5099 covers `value` falling outside `(min_value, max_value)`. This report is specifically about the bound-normalization statements corrupting `min_value`/`max_value` themselves.

title: Stray 's' in config deprecation warning also disables textwrap.dedent(), leaving the message indented
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

In `ConfigOption.set_value()`, the deprecation warning for a not-yet-expired config option opens its f-string with a stray `s` character:

```python
# lib/streamlit/config_option.py:285
get_logger(__name__).warning(
    textwrap.dedent(
        f"""s
        ════════════════════════════════════════════════
        {self.key} IS DEPRECATED.
```

This has two effects. The obvious one is a literal `s` printed at the start of the warning. The subtler one is that `textwrap.dedent()` silently stops working: `dedent` strips the longest common leading whitespace across all non-blank lines, and `s` is a line with **zero** indentation, so the common prefix becomes `""` and nothing is stripped. Every subsequent line keeps its 20 spaces of source indentation.

The sibling "expired" branch a few lines above is written correctly and dedents as intended, which makes the difference easy to see side by side.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import logging

from streamlit.config_option import ConfigOption

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s|%(message)s")

opt = ConfigOption(
    "test.notexpired",
    description="d",
    default_val="",
    deprecated=True,
    deprecation_text="Use something else.",
    expiration_date="2999-01-01",
)
opt.set_value("x", "some_file.toml")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the snippet above (any deprecated config option whose `expiration_date` is in the future takes this branch).
2. Compare the output with the expired branch (set `expiration_date="2020-01-01"`).

### Expected Behavior

The warning should be flush-left and free of stray characters, matching the expired-option message:

```
════════════════════════════════════════════════
test.notexpired IS DEPRECATED.
Use something else.

This option will be removed on or after 2999-01-01.

Please update some_file.toml.
════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

### Current Behavior

```
WARNING streamlit.config_option: s
                    ════════════════════════════════════════════════
                    test.notexpired IS DEPRECATED.
                    Use something else.

                    This option will be removed on or after 2999-01-01.

                    Please update some_file.toml.
                    ════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

For contrast, the expired branch on the same run is correct:

```
ERROR streamlit.config_option:
════════════════════════════════════════════════
test.expired IS NO LONGER SUPPORTED.

Use something else.

Please update some_file.toml.
════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

### Suggested Fix

Delete the stray `s` so the first line is empty and `dedent()` can compute the correct common prefix.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The deprecation warning contains no leading `s`.
- [ ] The warning body is dedented, matching the formatting of the expired-option error.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Unknown.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11 (platform-independent)
- Browser: n/a

### Additional Information

This branch is currently hard to hit in practice because the only deprecated option in `config.py` (`mapbox.token`) is already past its expiration date and therefore takes the *other* branch — see the companion issue about that expiry. Any newly added deprecation would surface this immediately.

title: StreamlitInvalidColorError message renders as one run-on line because bullets lack newlines
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

`StreamlitInvalidColorError` builds its message from implicitly concatenated string literals, but the literals that introduce the bullet list have no separating newline:

```python
# lib/streamlit/errors.py:589-592
"This does not look like a valid color: {color}.\n\n"
"Colors must be in one of the following formats:"
"* Hex string with 3, 4, 6, or 8 digits. Example: `'#00ff00'`"
"* List or tuple with 3 or 4 components. Example: `[1.0, 0.5, 0, 0.2]`",
```

Python concatenates these into a single line, so the two bullets never start a new line. Because the message is rendered as Markdown, the `*` characters do not become a list — they appear as literal asterisks mid-sentence.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st

st.map(
    {"lat": [37.77], "lon": [-122.4]},
    color="not-a-color",
)
```

Or directly:

```python
from streamlit.elements.lib.color_util import to_int_color_tuple

to_int_color_tuple("red")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Pass any invalid color to an API that validates colors (`st.map(color=...)`, `st.scatter_chart(color=...)`, etc.).
2. Read the resulting error message.

### Expected Behavior

```
This does not look like a valid color: 'red'.

Colors must be in one of the following formats:
* Hex string with 3, 4, 6, or 8 digits. Example: `'#00ff00'`
* List or tuple with 3 or 4 components. Example: `[1.0, 0.5, 0, 0.2]`
```

### Current Behavior

```
This does not look like a valid color: 'red'.

Colors must be in one of the following formats:* Hex string with 3, 4, 6, or 8 digits. Example: `'#00ff00'`* List or tuple with 3 or 4 components. Example: `[1.0, 0.5, 0, 0.2]`
```

### Suggested Fix

Append `\n` to the `"...following formats:"` literal and to the first bullet.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The error message renders as a Markdown bullet list in the app.
- [ ] The plain-text form contains one bullet per line.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Unknown.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11 (platform-independent)
- Browser: n/a

### Additional Information

I scanned the rest of `lib/streamlit/` for the same pattern (a string literal beginning `* ` or `- ` immediately following a literal that does not end in a newline) using a `tokenize`-based check; `errors.py:591-592` is the only occurrence, so this looks like an isolated slip rather than a systemic one.

title: mapbox.token deprecation expired 2026-05-01: logs "IS NO LONGER SUPPORTED" while the option still works
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

The `mapbox.token` config option is declared with `expiration_date="2026-05-01"`, which is now in the past. `ConfigOption.is_expired()` therefore returns `True`, and anyone who still sets the option is told it **is no longer supported** — at `ERROR` level — even though the option is still read and still works (`lib/streamlit/elements/map.py` passes it through to the PyDeck spec).

The result is a contradiction: the log says the setting has been removed, the product still honours it, and the message quotes a removal date that has already passed.

### Reproducible Code Example

`.streamlit/config.toml`:

```toml
[mapbox]
token = "pk.example"
```

Then start any app, or check the state directly:

```python
import streamlit.config as config

config.get_config_options()
opt = config._config_options_template["mapbox.token"]
print(opt.expiration_date, opt.is_expired())   # 2026-05-01 True
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Set `mapbox.token` in `config.toml` (or via `STREAMLIT_MAPBOX_TOKEN`).
2. Start the app and read the console.

### Expected Behavior

One of the following, consistently:

- The option is actually removed, and setting it is a no-op with a clear message; or
- The expiration date is moved out to a real future release, so users see the "IS DEPRECATED … will be removed on or after `<future date>`" warning instead.

### Current Behavior

```
════════════════════════════════════════════════
mapbox.token IS NO LONGER SUPPORTED.

Instead of this, you should use either the MAPBOX_API_KEY environment
variable or PyDeck's `api_keys` argument.

Please update <path to config.toml>.
════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

logged at `ERROR` level, while `config.get_option("mapbox.token")` still returns the token and `st.map` still uses it.

### Relevant Source

`lib/streamlit/config.py:1384-1398` declares the option; `lib/streamlit/config_option.py:262-297` selects the expired vs. not-expired message.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `mapbox.token` is either removed or given a future expiration date.
- [ ] The message users see matches whether the option actually still functions.
- [ ] Ideally, a test or CI check fails when a deprecated config option's `expiration_date` passes, so this does not drift again.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Not a regression — a deprecation that has quietly aged past its own deadline.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11 (platform-independent)
- Browser: n/a

### Additional Information

`mapbox.token` is currently the only deprecated option in `config.py`, so it is also the only one exercising this code path.

title: Python unit tests are not portable to Windows (path separators, NamedTemporaryFile reopen, registry-dependent MIME type)
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

Running the Python unit suite on Windows produces a large number of failures that are caused by the tests themselves rather than by the library. `CONTRIBUTING.md` does not restrict development to POSIX, so a contributor on Windows currently cannot use a green suite as a baseline.

This report covers three failures whose root cause I isolated precisely. (Two other clusters are excluded on purpose: the `write_test.py` / `help_test.py` failures belong to a separate library bug I filed about `is_mem_address_str`, and the `metrics_util_test.py` cluster is caused by the tests reading the developer's real home directory, which is a distinct test-isolation concern.)

### Steps To Reproduce

```console
$ uv run pytest lib/tests/ -q
```

on Windows.

### Failures and root causes

**1. `lib/tests/streamlit/components/v2/test_component_registry.py::test_resolve_glob_pattern_direct`**

The assertion compares a native path string against a POSIX-normalized one:

```python
assert str(resolved.resolve()) == Path(test_file).resolve().as_posix()
```

`str(Path)` yields `C:\Users\...\test-pattern.js` while `.as_posix()` yields `C:/Users/.../test-pattern.js`. These coincide only on POSIX.

```
AssertionError: assert 'C:\\Users\\a...st-pattern.js' == 'C:/Users/asu...st-pattern.js'
```

Fix: compare like with like — either `.as_posix()` on both sides or `Path(...) == Path(...)`.

**2. `lib/tests/streamlit/elements/video_test.py::VideoTest::test_st_video_subtitles_path`**

The test writes to a `NamedTemporaryFile` and, while it is still open, passes its path to `st.video(...)`, which reopens it. Windows does not permit reopening a still-open `NamedTemporaryFile`:

```
PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: 'C:\\Users\\...\\tmpyltckifk.vtt'
lib\streamlit\elements\lib\subtitle_utils.py:121: PermissionError
```

Fix: close the handle (or use `delete=False` / a `TemporaryDirectory`) before handing the path to code that opens it.

**3. `lib/tests/streamlit/elements/download_button_test.py::DownloadButtonTest::test_file_object_infers_file_name_and_mime`**

The test asserts a specific MIME type for `.csv`:

```
AssertionError: assert 'application/vnd.ms-excel' == 'text/csv'
```

`mimetypes.guess_type()` consults the Windows registry (`HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT`), where `.csv` is commonly mapped to `application/vnd.ms-excel` on machines with Excel installed. The expected value therefore depends on the host's registry rather than on Streamlit.

Fix: register the expected mapping in the test (or in library setup) via `mimetypes.add_type("text/csv", ".csv")`, or assert against `mimetypes.guess_type` rather than a hard-coded string.

### Expected Behavior

`uv run pytest lib/tests/` passes on Windows, or the supported development platforms are stated explicitly in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

### Current Behavior

A full run reports **59 distinct test failures (95 including subtests)**, of which the three above are cleanly attributable to non-portable test code.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The three tests above pass on Windows without weakening what they assert.
- [ ] Optionally, a Windows job in CI (even a subset) to keep the suite portable.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Unknown.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11
- Browser: n/a

### Additional Information

Happy to split these into separate issues or open a PR for the three fixes if that is preferred.

title: Broken relative link in .github/copilot-instructions.md and stale knip ignoreDependencies entries
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

Two small repository-hygiene defects found while auditing the tree.

**1. Broken relative link in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`**

Line 88 reads:

```markdown
- See [.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md](.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md) for the full debugging guide.
```

The file lives in `.github/`, so the relative link resolves to `.github/.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md`, which does not exist. The real file is at the repository root: `.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md`.

This text is duplicated from `AGENTS.md`, where the same relative link is correct because that file sits at the root — the copy into `.github/` did not adjust the path.

Fix: use `../.claude/skills/debugging-streamlit/SKILL.md` (or a root-absolute link).

**2. Stale `ignoreDependencies` entries in `frontend/knip.json`**

`yarn knip` reports three entries that are no longer needed:

```
Configuration hints (3)
@deck.gl/extensions          knip.json  Remove from ignoreDependencies
@deck.gl/widgets             knip.json  Remove from ignoreDependencies
react-responsive-carousel    knip.json  Remove from ignoreDependencies
```

These suppressions now hide nothing, so keeping them only reduces the value of the check.

Fix: drop the three entries.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Open `.github/copilot-instructions.md` on GitHub and click the link on line 88 — it 404s.
2. Run `yarn knip` in `frontend/` and read the "Configuration hints" section.

### Expected Behavior

- The documentation link resolves to the skill file.
- `yarn knip` reports no configuration hints.

### Current Behavior

- The link 404s.
- Three stale hints are reported on every run.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The link in `.github/copilot-instructions.md` resolves correctly from its own directory.
- [ ] `yarn knip` reports no configuration hints.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11
- Browser: n/a

### Additional Information

I checked every relative Markdown link in the repository (171 files) for this class of problem; `.github/copilot-instructions.md:88` is the only genuinely broken one. The other candidates were either illustrative syntax examples in the `developing-with-streamlit` skill docs or a spec referencing a path that was never created.

title: Frontend uses user-controlled file name as FormData field name in file upload
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

In `uploadFileUploaderFile`, the frontend constructs a `FormData` object for file uploads using the file's own name (`name`) as the multipart form-data field name: `form.append(name, file, fileName)`. Because the backend does not rely on this dynamic field name and files are uploaded individually, using the user-controlled filename introduces potential security risks, such as bypassing security filters, WAFs, or length restrictions designed for form field names.


```typescript
const form = new FormData()
const { name, webkitRelativePath } = file
// For directory uploads, use the relative path as fileName to preserve directory structure
const fileName = webkitRelativePath || name
form.append(name, file, fileName)

```

### Proposed Solution

Replace the dynamic `name` variable with a static string (such as `"file"`), since files are handled individually and the backend does not require the field name to match the filename.

```typescript
const form = new FormData()
const { name, webkitRelativePath } = file
// For directory uploads, use the relative path as fileName to preserve directory structure
const fileName = webkitRelativePath || name
form.append("file", file, fileName)

```


### Security Impact

* **User-Controlled Field Names:** Attackers can manipulate file names (including special characters, injection sequences, or excessive lengths) which are then directly injected into the multipart form-data structure as the field name.
* **Validation & WAF Bypasses:** Backend proxies, Web Application Firewalls (WAFs), or API gateways often enforce strict validation rules (character sets, maximum length) on form field names. Allowing client-side filenames to define these keys can lead to unexpected parsing behavior or security filter evasion.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

uploaded_file = st.file_uploader("Choose a file")
if uploaded_file is not None:
    st.write(f"Uploaded filename: {uploaded_file.name}")
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the provided Python script using Streamlit.
2. Open your browser's Developer Tools and navigate to the **Network** tab.
3. Upload a file via the file uploader (e.g., a file named `malicious_name_test.txt`).
4. Inspect the multipart `form-data` payload sent in the upload request.
5. Observe that the form field `name` attribute equals the file's name (`malicious_name_test.txt`) instead of a static, controlled identifier.

### Expected Behavior

The multipart form-data request should use a static, predefined field name (such as `name="file"`) for the upload payload, ensuring that the form field name is fully controlled and sanitized, while the actual file name/path remains properly preserved only in the filename parameter.

### Current Behavior

When a file is uploaded through `st.file_uploader`, the frontend dynamically sets the multipart form-data field name to match the uploaded file's name (`form.append(name, file, fileName)`). As a result, user-controlled strings, special characters, and arbitrary lengths are directly injected into the request's form field name.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.58.0
- Python version: 3.11
- Operating System: Windows
- Browser: Chrome


### Additional Information

_No response_

title: st.file_uploader hangs indefinitely on small files when sentry_sdk.init() runs in-process before Streamlit starts
body:
**Summary**

File uploads under ~10KB hang indefinitely (eventually timing out client-side) when `sentry_sdk.init()` is called in the same process, before Streamlit's own event loop is created, and Streamlit is then started in that process (e.g. via `streamlit.web.cli.main()` after rewriting `sys.argv`, rather than a fresh `streamlit run` subprocess). Uploads over ~10KB are unaffected. This reproduces with no application code beyond a single `st.file_uploader()`.

This in-process launch pattern is common for wrapper entrypoints that do setup (init error tracking, run DB migrations, etc.) before starting Streamlit without spawning a new OS process.

**Reproducible Code Example**

```python
"""
pip install streamlit==1.61.1 sentry-sdk==2.61.1
python repro.py
Then open http://localhost:8501 and upload a file smaller than ~10KB.
"""
import sys
import pathlib

pathlib.Path("app.py").write_text('''
import streamlit as st
uploaded = st.file_uploader("pick a file")
if uploaded is not None:
    st.write(f"Got {uploaded.name}, {len(uploaded.getvalue())} bytes")
''')

import sentry_sdk
sentry_sdk.init(dsn=None)  # comment this line out and the hang disappears

from streamlit.web import cli
sys.argv = ["streamlit", "run", "app.py"]
sys.exit(cli.main())
```

**Steps To Reproduce**

1. `pip install streamlit==1.61.1 sentry-sdk==2.61.1`
2. Save the snippet above as `repro.py`, run `python repro.py`
3. Open `http://localhost:8501`, upload any file smaller than ~10KB (e.g. a 300-byte CSV)
4. Upload hangs indefinitely. Comment out `sentry_sdk.init(dsn=None)` and it succeeds instantly. Upload a file larger than ~10KB and it succeeds either way.

**Expected Behavior**

Upload completes regardless of file size or whether Sentry was initialized in-process before Streamlit started.

**Current Behavior**

Small uploads hang. Root-caused to Sentry's `StarletteIntegration` (enabled by default) — confirmed via `sentry_sdk.init(dsn=None, disabled_integrations=[StarletteIntegration()])` (succeeds) vs. `disabled_integrations=[ThreadingIntegration()]` (still hangs — ruling out threading despite superficial similarity to #15374 / #16139, both of which are already fixed in this version and don't apply since this repro has no `st.fragment(run_every=...)`). `StarletteIntegration` instruments Starlette's ASGI request lifecycle, and the hang lives inside Starlette's own multipart parser — Sentry wraps exactly the layer that breaks.

**Is this a regression?**

Not tested on older versions — can test if useful.

**Debug info**

- Streamlit version: 1.61.1
- Python version: 3.12
- OS: macOS (also reproduces in a Linux container)
- sentry-sdk version: 2.61.1

**Additional Information**

Fuller repro with isolation scripts (control, all-integrations-disabled, Starlette-only-disabled) and sample CSVs: https://gist.github.com/tbrambor/d41b40950a0061ca404fc0d67e4768ed

operating_system.value: macOS (also reproduces in a Linux container)

title: Nested run_every fragment stays on screen with stale content after being hidden
body:
### Checklist


### Summary

When a nested `run_every` fragment stops being rendered, its container can stay on screen showing frozen, stale content until the *enclosing* fragment next completes a run. Because the enclosing fragment has no timer of its own, that means it stays visible until the user next interacts with it.

The cause is on the frontend: the enclosing fragment's run finishes successfully and schedules the usual stale-node cleanup, but that cleanup executes with a *later* run's `scriptRunId`/`fragmentIdsThisRun`, so it is scoped to the wrong fragment and never prunes the evicted subtree.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
from uuid import uuid4

import streamlit as st


@st.fragment(run_every=1.0)
def standalone_auto():
    with st.container(key="standalone_auto_fragment"):
        st.write(f"uuid in fragment: {uuid4()}")


standalone_auto()


@st.fragment
def outer():
    show_nested = st.checkbox("Show nested auto fragment", value=True)
    if show_nested:

        @st.fragment
        def middle():
            @st.fragment(run_every=1.0)
            def nested_auto():
                with st.container(key="nested_auto_fragment"):
                    st.write(f"nested uuid: {uuid4()}")

            nested_auto()

        middle()


outer()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app above and wait a few seconds so both `run_every` fragments are ticking.
2. Uncheck "Show nested auto fragment".
3. Repeat, toggling at varying moments relative to the 1s tick. Under CPU load it reproduces roughly once every 4-6 attempts; on an idle machine it is rare.

It is timing sensitive: the toggle has to land while the standalone fragment's next auto-rerun is arriving. Note that `console.log`-based instrumentation slows message handling enough to hide it — use an in-page array if you need to trace.

### Expected Behavior

Unchecking the box removes the nested fragment's container, as it does on a normal rerun.

### Current Behavior

The `nested_auto_fragment` container stays in the DOM with its last-rendered content. It does not update again (its auto-rerun timer is correctly cancelled by `stop_auto_rerun`), so it reads as stale data rather than an obviously broken element. It clears on a full rerun, or when the enclosing fragment next completes a run — which for a timer-less fragment means the next user interaction with it.

Also seen in CI as a flake in `st_fragment_run_every_test.py::test_nested_fragment_run_every_can_hide_without_crash` (e.g. https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/actions/runs/33181944052), failing with `Locator expected not to be attached`.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Not a regression of #15130. That fixed the white-screen crash in this same scenario (#15084); this leftover-element behavior is a separate defect in the same area.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`)
- Python version: 3.11.6
- Operating System: macOS 26.6.2
- Browser: reproduced on WebKit; not browser specific

### Additional Information

**Root cause (verified by instrumenting the frontend).** `handleScriptFinished` schedules stale-node cleanup inside a `setState` updater that reads `scriptRunId` and `fragmentIdsThisRun` from `prevState` (`frontend/app/src/App.tsx:2027-2038`). Under load the next fragment run has already been committed by the time that updater flushes, so the cleanup runs for the wrong run. Captured trace, with the scheduling status paired against the state the updater actually saw:

```
delta addBlock   frag=28b54e path=0.1   run=6bd090          <- enclosing fragment writes
delta newElement frag=28b54e path=0.1.0 run=6bd090
scriptFinished ENTRY status=FINISHED_FRAGMENT_RUN_SUCCESSFULLY
                     entryRun=6bd090 entryFrags=28b54e      <- its run, finished successfully
delta ... frag=f81f56 run=af93e8                            <- next (standalone) run starts
cleanup scheduledBy=FINISHED_FRAGMENT_RUN_SUCCESSFULLY
        SEES run=af93e8 frags=f81f56                        <- executed as the standalone run
```

So the cleanup ran as `clearStaleNodes(af93e8, ["f81f56"])`. `ClearStaleNodeVisitor` therefore never descended into the enclosing fragment's subtree at `0.1` with `fragmentIdOfBlock` set, and the evicted container was never pruned.

Worth noting the run finished `FINISHED_FRAGMENT_RUN_SUCCESSFULLY`, **not** `FINISHED_EARLY_FOR_RERUN` — so this is not the deliberate cleanup skip for interrupted runs.

**Why this probably needs a server-side change.** `ForwardMsg.script_finished` is a bare enum (`proto/streamlit/proto/ForwardMsg.proto:46-57`, `:66`) and carries no run identity, so the client can only infer which run finished from React state. Both readings are unreliable, in opposite directions, and I observed each failing in the same session:

- at flush time it can see a *later* run (the failure above);
- at handler entry it can see an *earlier* run, when several messages are handled before a commit.

Carrying the run id (and `fragment_ids_this_run`) on `ScriptFinished` so cleanup can be pinned to the run that actually finished would fix it at the source.

**One constraint for whoever picks this up.** A frontend-only workaround that *removes* the evicted nodes is unsafe. Deltas address nodes by absolute path, and `AppRoot.addBlock` inherits an existing block's children rather than resetting them, so removing a node compacts its parent's `children` and every later sibling keeps the shifted index. A fragment sibling that reruns on its own then writes to the wrong slot — I reproduced a silent duplication (`["live"]` → later delta at its original path `[0, 1]` → `["live", "live v2"]`), and `SetNodeByDeltaPathVisitor` can escalate the same shift to a `Bad delta path index` throw. Substituting an index-preserving empty block avoids that, but does not address the attribution race itself. Explored in #16705, which is closed in favour of this issue.

**Related:** #15084, #15130 (the crash in this scenario), #10805 (widget-state cleanup with `run_every`).

title: Add `st.column_config.DurationColumn` for timedelta / duration values
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a dedicated `st.column_config.DurationColumn` as the first-class column type for `datetime.timedelta` / `pandas.Timedelta` / Arrow duration values. It should own duration-specific display formats, `min`/`max`/`step` as timedeltas, and a real duration editor. `TimeColumn` should stay clock-of-day only; `NumberColumn` can remain the escape hatch for “treat this duration as seconds.”

### Why?

Timedelta is elapsed time (negatives, multi-day, 336 hours). That is a different type from:

- **`TimeColumn`**: clock-of-day. HTML `<input type="time">`, `min`/`max` as `datetime.time`, wraps at 24h, string sort. Read-only rendering only looks right for the narrow case of a positive duration under 24 hours (`1s` → `00:00:01`). Everything else is a silent lie (`14 days` wraps or fakes `336:00:00`; negatives have no representation). That is the same class of bug as #9751 (`1s` shown as `00:16:40`). If `TimeColumn` cannot represent a value, it should error rather than show a wrong clock time.
- **`NumberColumn`**: numeric sort and printf formats. Good enough as a v1 for display + sort (#8949), including `format="clock"` for an elapsed-time clock. It is a leaky API for durations: `min`/`max`/`step` are raw seconds, and the editor is a number spinner on `7200`.

A dedicated type is what pays off once we want a real duration API: discoverable config, a format namespace that is not a number format, timedelta-typed bounds, and an editor that is not “type 7200 to mean 2 hours.”

### How?

```python
st.dataframe(
    df,
    column_config={
        "latency": st.column_config.DurationColumn(
            format="duration",  # humanize, default
            min_value=datetime.timedelta(0),
            max_value=datetime.timedelta(days=14),
            step=datetime.timedelta(seconds=1),
        ),
        "runtime": st.column_config.DurationColumn(format="clock"),
    },
)
```

**Default mapping:** Arrow duration / pandas timedelta → `DurationColumn` (read-only until editing ships). Keep `NumberColumn` as the opt-in for numeric / printf formats on seconds.

**Do not reuse `TimeColumn`.** Do not send nanosecond ticks to JS (overflows `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` after ~104 days). Wire format should stay **seconds as a float**; Python applies `pd.Timedelta(seconds=value)` so pandas writes the column’s native unit (`us` on pandas 3, `ns` on pandas 2). Strings can stay as a fallback (`pd.Timedelta("2 hours")`).

**Editing, in order of cost / quality:**

1. **Text parse (best first editor).** Overlay is a text field. Accept the same strings pandas already understands: `"2 hours"`, `"1 day 03:00:00"`, `"00:00:01"`, `"P2DT3H"`, `"-3 days"`. Display can stay humanized or clock; the committed value is still seconds (or a normalized string). Handles negatives and multi-day.
2. **Custom elapsed-time overlay (best UX).** Glide custom cell: optional days + `HH:mm:ss`, hours not wrapped at 24, optional sign. `min`/`max`/`step` are timedeltas. This is the main reason for `DurationColumn` to exist rather than piggyback on `NumberColumn`.
3. **Number + unit.** Spinner plus s/min/h/d. Fine as a power-user option, poor as the default for mixed-scale columns.
4. **`NumberColumn(disabled=False)`.** Already works as an escape hatch (edits raw seconds). Not product-quality as the default editor.

Suggested `format` values (duration namespace, not number formats): `"duration"` (humanize, default), `"clock"` (elapsed clock, hours not wrapped at 24), `"localized"` (Intl.DurationFormat), maybe ISO `PT2H` later.

### Additional Context

Related:

- #8949 — timedelta sort used the humanized string (`14 days`, `2 hours`, `a day`) instead of the underlying value. Fixed by mapping duration → `NumberColumn` with values stored as seconds.
- #9751 — `TimeColumn` on `pd.Timedelta` showed a wrong clock time. `TimeColumn` should keep erroring on duration; the clock display belongs on `DurationColumn` / `NumberColumn(format="clock")`.

Display + numeric sort do not require this type. Add `DurationColumn` when we want first-class editing or a cleaner public API.

title: Minimize `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` errors
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Reduce how often developers hit `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` (duplicate widget/element ID) errors by making element ID generation smarter about the surrounding container context — so that identical widgets placed in different containers (chat messages, fragments, columns, etc.) don't collide without the developer having to manually craft unique `key`s everywhere.

### Why?

It's increasingly common to have repeating identical widgets across different chat messages, fragment calls, or columns. Today the developer must manage and track a unique `key` for each, which adds a lot of boilerplate and complexity. This is especially painful in chat/LLM apps (in-chat interactive widgets, code-eval "run" buttons, generated suggestion buttons) — and for LLM-generated code it can be nearly impossible to solve, since the model may emit duplicate widgets across messages. `st.form` already avoids this within forms (the `form_id` is part of the ID), which shows the approach can work more broadly.

This is a high-impact papercut: `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` is the **No. 3 most thrown uncaught exception type**, occurring in ~**0.5% of all apps**.

A related pain point: some elements raise `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` and tell you to add a `key`, but **don't actually support a `key` argument**, leaving no clean fix. Examples:
- #11424 — showing the same `st.plotly_chart` multiple times raises `StreamlitDuplicateElementId`.
- #11360 — multiple `st.audio` calls with the same parameters and `autoplay=True` raise a duplicate error that prompts you to add a key, but `st.audio` has no `key`.

### How?

Incorporate more of the container context into an element's ID computation, focusing on **stable, explicit signals** (not user-facing text). Ideas:

- **Wrapping container keys:** automatically include the `key` of wrapping containers / `st.fragment` / `st.form` (those that support keys) in the child element's ID computation. Only for containers that have an explicit key set.
  - If we do this, it strengthens the case for **adding `key` to more containers and elements** — see #9580 and the concrete cases #11424 (`st.plotly_chart`) and #11360 (`st.audio`), plus #6152.
- **Re-evaluate key namespaces and parent-key reuse:** regular element keys, form IDs, and fragment definition keys are currently tracked in separate registries. `st.form` already contributes its `form_id` to the auto-generated IDs of unkeyed children; fragment keys identify fragment definitions but are not currently part of regular child element ID computation. Consider both:
  - Reusing explicit form / fragment / keyed-container keys as stable parent context for **unkeyed** descendants.
  - Whether form and fragment keys should participate in the same duplicate-key checks as regular element keys, or remain separate namespaces that only contribute parent context.

  Treat registry unification as a compatibility decision: the same string can currently be reused between some form / fragment and regular-element keys, and one keyed fragment definition can intentionally run from multiple call sites. Preserve the rule that an explicit child `key` is authoritative and independent of its container.
- **Column index in `st.columns`:** include the column number in the ID computation so the same widget in different columns of the same `st.columns` call doesn't collide.
- **Parent container types:** include the parent container type(s) as part of the ID computation.

**Important caution — be conservative about what goes into ID generation.** Adding container context to the ID changes element identity, which has a subtle downside: a widget that **dynamically moves between containers** (e.g. its wrapping container changes across reruns) would get a new ID and thus lose its identity and state. This is the main risk to weigh (more so than existing widget state resetting on upgrade), and it can be fixed by explicitly setting a `key` on that element so its identity no longer depends on the container context. In particular:
- **Do not** include user-facing **labels/titles** of wrapping containers (e.g. expander label, dialog title, popover label, tab name) in the ID — these change often and would be fragile/surprising. Prefer **explicitly set keys** for disambiguation instead.
- Auto-added context must apply **only to widgets without an explicit `key`**. When a user sets an explicit `key="x"`, the ID must **not** include the added container context — an explicit key should always behave predictably and stay stable regardless of the surrounding containers. Think through backwards compatibility / migration carefully.

### Additional Context

- Add `key` to more elements/containers: #9580, and concrete duplicate-ID cases where no `key` is available today: #11424 (`st.plotly_chart`), #11360 (`st.audio`).
- Related: #6152 (composable/reusable component API for larger apps).
- `st.form` already includes `form_id` in widget ID generation — a useful precedent.
- There is an older internal product spec exploring options (implicit container key-prefix, adding `key`/`key_prefix` to containers, best-practice docs, or fixing duplicate IDs via enumeration). This issue intentionally leans toward the conservative, explicit-key-based approaches from that discussion.

title: Modernize `st.chat_message` design to match modern agentic chat UIs
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Refresh the visual design and interaction model of `st.chat_message` so chat/agentic apps look modern out of the box — closer to the chat UIs people expect from tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and other assistants. This includes rethinking avatars, message alignment, per-message actions, and how the message background is themed.

### Why?

`st.chat_message` is central to Streamlit's most compelling demos (LLM/agentic apps), but its default look feels dated compared to modern chat UIs. Users routinely reach for CSS hacks or custom components to get a contemporary look (hidden avatars, right-aligned user bubbles, hover actions). Making the default modern — and the common tweaks first-class — would make agentic apps look polished with no effort and reduce reliance on fragile workarounds.

### How?

Modernize the design and add a few high-value options, for example:

- **Avatars:** make the design look clean when avatars are hidden, and consider hiding them by default (or an easy option to hide them). Today an avatar is always shown.
- **User vs. assistant alignment:** support right-aligned user messages (bubble style) and left-aligned assistant messages, matching common chat UIs.
- **Per-message actions:** built-in, hover-revealed actions on a message (e.g. copy, thumbs up/down, regenerate, custom actions) that can trigger callbacks/reruns.
- **General styling refresh:** spacing, bubble/background treatment, and typography that feel modern and cohesive with the rest of the app theme.

**Background & nested-element theming:** Apply the message background via **theming** and update nested elements so they render correctly against it — like the **sidebar** does. Using the **secondary background color** is a promising approach (nested elements already look right in the sidebar), and it should also fix cases like charts not looking good against the current gray background. This is closely related to the background handling in the [`st.container` background/shadow spec (#14683)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/14683).

Keep everything backwards compatible (opt-in where it changes existing looks) and themeable.

- [Figma Mockups](https://www.figma.com/design/fzBM3vuV1Dh0lznSzKxOh4/Streamlit-Open-Source-design-system?node-id=3973-16463&t=waRdSwMGoWbMj4A1-4)

### Additional Context

Related issues to fold into this modernization:
- #10740 — configurable toolbar / clickable actions on `st.chat_message`.
- #6921 — "Copy to Clipboard" button in `st.chat_message`.
- #11380 — color and background color support for `st.chat_message` avatars.

title: Deprecate widget callback `args`/`kwargs` in favor of `functools.partial`
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Deprecate the `args` and `kwargs` parameters that widgets currently expose for passing arguments to `on_change` / `on_click` callbacks, and recommend `functools.partial` instead. As part of this, support automatically receiving relevant state (e.g. the widget's new value) in the callback, as requested in #5305.

### Why?

- **Redundant API surface:** `args`/`kwargs` exist on essentially every widget purely to forward arguments to callbacks. Python already has a standard, well-understood tool for this — `functools.partial` — so `args`/`kwargs` are extra parameters to learn, document, and maintain on every widget for something the language handles natively.
- **Consistency & simplicity:** removing them shrinks the signature of every widget and aligns with "prefer Pythonic idioms" and "extend/compose over inventing".
- **Better ergonomics for callbacks:** today callbacks often have to read `st.session_state` to find out what value changed, which makes generic reusable handlers awkward. Passing the value (and possibly key) to the callback automatically (#5305) removes that friction.

### How?

- **Recommend `functools.partial`** as the replacement for `args`/`kwargs`:

```python
from functools import partial

def update(param_name, *, value):
    ...

st.selectbox("Pick", options, on_change=partial(update, "selection_1"))
```

- **Deprecate `args`/`kwargs`** on widgets with a long, clearly-communicated deprecation window and docs/migration guidance (they keep working during the deprecation period). See API principle "Graceful Evolution" (3+ months notice, clear migration path).
- **Auto-pass state to callbacks** (#5305): make the widget's new value available to the callback automatically (e.g. as a keyword argument), so reusable/generic handlers don't need to reach into `st.session_state`. The exact mechanism needs design (opt-in signature detection vs. a fixed kwarg) to stay backwards compatible.

### Additional Context

- Incorporates #5305 (pass state as a parameter to the `on_change` callback).
- This is a cross-cutting change affecting all widgets with callbacks (`on_change`/`on_click`), so it warrants a spec and careful, gradual deprecation.

title: Add a link/bookmark element that renders a rich link preview card
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a link/bookmark element that renders a URL as a rich preview card — with properties like an icon/favicon, title, description, and optionally a preview image — similar to how a bookmark looks in Notion or a link result in Google search. It could optionally **auto-fetch** these properties (e.g. from the page's Open Graph / metadata) when they aren't provided explicitly, and it should **adapt its layout** based on which properties are present.

### Why?

Links are everywhere in apps (sources, references, related resources, docs), but a bare Markdown link is visually flat. A rich, consistent link/bookmark card makes references look polished and scannable — great for dashboards, research/agent apps that cite sources, resource lists, and "read more" sections. Today users hand-build these with columns + images + markdown or custom components, which is fiddly and inconsistent.

### How?

A new element, e.g.:

```python
st.link_preview(
    "https://streamlit.io",
    title="Streamlit • A faster way to build and share data apps",
    description="Streamlit is an open-source Python framework for data scientists and AI/ML engineers to deliver interactive data apps – in only a few lines of code.",
    icon="https://streamlit.io/favicon.png",   # icon/favicon
    image="https://.../preview.png",           # optional large preview image
)

# Minimal — auto-fetch metadata from the URL:
st.link_preview("https://streamlit.io")
```

Behavior:
- **Dynamic layout:** adapt the card to whichever properties are provided — e.g. compact (favicon + title + description) vs. a larger card with a preview image (like the two reference looks below).
- **Auto-fetch (optional):** when title/description/icon/image aren't given, fetch them from the target URL's metadata (Open Graph / `<meta>` / favicon). Should be opt-in-friendly and degrade gracefully if fetching fails or is blocked (fall back to just the URL/title). Consider caching and the SiS/Community-Cloud implications of server-side fetching (and whether fetching happens backend- or frontend-side).
- Whole card is a link to the URL; supports opening in a new tab.

**Alternative / complementary: a Markdown directive.** This could also be exposed as a Markdown directive so bookmarks can be embedded inline in any markdown text (e.g. `st.markdown`), for example:

```
:bookmark[https://python-markdown.github.io/extensions/toc/]{title="Foo" icon=":material/info:"}
```

The directive attributes (`title`, `description`, `icon`, `image`, …) map to the same properties as the element, and unspecified ones can be auto-fetched. A directive plays nicely with LLM-generated content and lets bookmarks appear inline within larger blocks of text.

**Simpler inline "mentions".** The same directive family could also cover a lighter-weight inline link — not a full card, but a link that doesn't use the default link color and instead has a more button-like hover effect, with a configurable icon and title. For example:

```
:mention[URL]{text="My link"}
:mention[URL]{text="My link" icon="🍀"}
:mention[URL]{text="My link" icon="github"}
:mention[URL]{icon="streamlit"}
```

This gives a compact, chip/mention-style link (great inline in text or chat) that sits between a plain Markdown link and the full bookmark card.

Reference looks (a compact link result vs. a larger card with a preview image):

- Compact: favicon + site + bold title (link color) + description snippet.
- Rich: title + description on the left, with a preview image on the right and favicon + URL at the bottom.

### Additional Context

- Inspired by link/bookmark cards in Notion and rich link results in Google search.
- Complements a possible OEmbed feature (embedding Streamlit content elsewhere); this is the inverse — richly embedding external links inside a Streamlit app.
- Related: #11990 (file chip element, e.g. for `st.chat_message`) — a similar compact, reference-style element that could share design/infrastructure.

title: Add a developer debug pane for inspecting state, cache, memory, and profiling
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a built-in developer "debug pane" — a panel (e.g. a collapsible sidebar/overlay) that surfaces debug information and dev tools without cluttering the main app. It would visualize `st.session_state` and cache contents, show memory usage and profiling/performance info, and provide a place to dump debug output (`st.help`, variables, etc.). By default it would be visible only to the app developer (not viewers), so developers don't have to comment debug code in and out.

### Why?

Debugging Streamlit apps today means peppering the main UI with `st.write(st.session_state)`, `st.help(...)`, timing prints, etc., then remembering to remove them. There's no first-class way to inspect what's actually going on — state, cache, memory, timings — in a dedicated, developer-only surface. A debug pane (à la [Django Debug Toolbar](https://github.com/jazzband/django-debug-toolbar)) would make development and troubleshooting dramatically easier and keep debug output out of the real app for end users.

### How?

A developer-only container/panel that is disabled by default for viewers other than the app developer. Over time it could host focused tools, for example:

- **State inspector:** visualize `st.session_state` contents.
- **Cache inspector:** visualize `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource` contents (and allow clearing).
- **Memory profiling:** memory usage, and how it changes run-over-run.
- **Execution/performance profiling:** time between/within widget calls and functions; distribution of run times run-over-run (e.g. via a profiler like yappi + a viewer like snakeviz).
- **Debug output container:** a scratch area to write `st.help`, dump variables, etc., that doesn't appear in the main window.
- **Variable inspector:** e.g. a selectbox + `st.help`.
- **Element/DOM inspector:** which widgets were rendered, and their inputs/values; last forward/back message (or equivalent).
- **Console logs** and **error context**.
- Possibly a **Python console** at the end of the app to run quick calculations/inspections (like a Jupyter interactive debugger).

Considerations:
- Developer-only visibility by default (not shown to app viewers); tie into a development vs. production mode.
- Start minimal (state + cache inspection) and grow over time.

### Additional Context

- Prior art: [Django Debug Toolbar](https://github.com/jazzband/django-debug-toolbar), [streamlit-forum](https://github.com/snehankekre/streamlit-forum).
- Closely related: #16306 (dedicated development and production modes) — this debug pane is a natural home for the "development mode" dev tools described there.

title: `setTriggerValue` called during mount is dropped ~1 in 4 times when the component remounts, despite an explicit `key`
body:
### Summary

When a Components V2 component calls `setTriggerValue` during mount (inside the default function, rather than from a user event handler), values are silently lost if the component remounts because its `data` changed — even when an explicit `key` is passed, which keeps the element id stable.

Measured roughly a quarter loss: **5 of 21 values sent were never received by Python at all.** They are not late — a scan of the entire session log shows they never arrive in any subsequent run.

This is split out of #14710, where it surfaced during investigation. It is distinct from the two by-design mechanisms discussed there (`data` participating in element identity for unkeyed components, and trigger values resetting after each run).

**Update — measured root cause.** A frontend race in `WidgetStateManager.removeInactive`: it destroys the synthetic trigger-aggregator widget state while that state is still awaiting its batched flush, so the app reruns with no trigger at all. Not a backend discard. Measured on a production build with the repro below: 10/85 values lost unpatched vs 0/85 patched, and with instrumentation, 14/14 losses correlated exactly with the destroying call. Mechanism and open question under Additional Information.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st

comp = st.components.v2.component(
    "repro.mount_trigger",
    js="""
    export default function (component) {
        const v = "val" + component.data.nonce;
        console.log("SEND " + v);
        component.setTriggerValue("v", v);
    }
    """,
)

if "clicks" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.clicks = 0
if st.button("bump"):
    st.session_state.clicks += 1

nonce = f"c{st.session_state.clicks}"
result = comp(data={"nonce": nonce}, key="stable_key")

received = result.get("v")
st.write(f"data nonce {nonce} -> received {received!r}")
print(f"nonce={nonce} received={received!r}", flush=True)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the app and open the browser console.
2. Click **bump** ~20 times, letting the app settle between clicks. Each click changes `data`, so the component remounts and sends one value.
3. Compare the `SEND val…` lines in the console against the `received=…` lines in the terminal.
4. Roughly one in four sent values never appears on the Python side.

### Expected Behavior

Every value the mounted component sends is readable on the following script run. The explicit `key` makes the element id stable, so a changing `data` payload should not affect delivery.

### Current Behavior

About 25% of values are never delivered. Verified as lost rather than late by scanning the full backend log after all clicks — 0 arrived in a later run.

The element id was logged each run and confirmed identical throughout (`$$ID-b4c118c7288cf7d656c205e58a384db6-stable_key`), so this is not the identity churn that affects unkeyed components.

Three controls on the same harness came out clean. They do not isolate the bug to trigger-on-mount — see Additional Information — but they do narrow which write path is affected:

| Variant | Result |
|---|---|
| `setStateValue` on mount, same conditions | 21/21 delivered |
| `setTriggerValue` from a user event handler, stable `data` | 20/20 delivered |
| `setTriggerValue` from a user event handler, churning `data` | 20/20 delivered |
| **`setTriggerValue` on mount, churning `data`** | **5 of 21 lost** |

### Additional Information

**Mechanism.** `setTriggerValue` writes to a synthetic aggregator widget id (`makeTriggerAggregatorId` → `$$STREAMLIT_INTERNAL_KEY_<componentId>__events`) and the flush is deferred to a `setTimeout(…, 0)` macrotask. `App.removeInactiveWidgetState()` runs from the `ScriptFinished` → `clearStaleNodes` setState callback and deletes every widget state whose id is not an active *element* id — the aggregator id never is, because it isn't part of the element tree. When that lands before the flush, the trigger is deleted but the rerun is still sent (`sendUpdateWidgetsMessage` uses unfiltered `createWidgetStatesMsg()`), so the script reruns with no trigger.

Mount-time triggers are the most exposed path: the component's `default function` runs behind `await loadAndRunModule(...)` (dynamic `import()` of a blob URL), so it executes a macrotask or more after the commit that mounted it. This also explains the control table — `setStateValue` is immune because it writes the component's real element id, and the event-handler controls passed because letting the app settle means `removeInactive` has already run.

**The `_pending_resets` theory is ruled out.** It is only populated by `mark_page_switch_drops`, which runs on page transitions and skips widgets whose recorded page is the current page, so a single-page app never populates it. (For the record, the original hypothesis was that `_pending_resets` in `lib/streamlit/runtime/state/session_state.py` discarded a frontend-resent value on re-registration, which would have made this by design.)

**Related blind spot.** The same synthetic id is invisible to other active-id filters, not just this one: `App.tsx` `onPageChange` sends `getActiveWidgetStates(activeWidgetIds)`, which would likewise drop a pending aggregator. Reaching it would require a trigger and a page navigation in the same macrotask, and dropping a trigger while navigating away is defensible, so no change is planned there. Recorded as an observation only.

**Scope of what was tested.** Measured against this repro on one machine, 235 trials total. It establishes this race as the cause of the loss seen here; it does not rule out other trigger-loss paths. The same race also appears to explain the recurring `bidi_components/basics_test.py::test_trigger_interactions` CI flake — the failure signature (counts unchanged plus `Result` reset to `None`) is what a trigger-less rerun produces — but that link is inferred from the signature, not directly observed. Two prior automated PRs (#14542, #14843) misattributed that flake to a slow iframe round-trip and raised timeouts.

**Open question for Components V2** (replacing the original question here, which is now answered — the drop is a race, not intentional): should `setTriggerValue` during mount be a supported pattern at all? Fixing the race makes it reliable, but it fires on every remount, so churning `data` produces one trigger per remount. That is a semantics decision independent of this bug, and it determines whether this issue closes as fixed or splits into a fix plus a documentation/warning change.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (released wheel, production frontend build)
- Python version: 3.11 · macOS · Chromium
- The ~25% figure is one 21-trial sample on a single machine; treat it as "roughly a quarter" rather than a precise rate.

streamlit_version.evidence_text: - Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (released wheel, production frontend build)

title: Runtime errors in Streamlit apps on HF Spaces rose 12.4% → 31.7% for the 2026 cohort while other SDKs fell
body:
Not a reproducible bug report — a signal from population data that may point at one, and I can't tell from the outside whether the cause is Streamlit or the Hugging Face runtime image.

I enumerated the complete public Hugging Face Spaces catalogue (1,458,692 Spaces) using the `runtime.stage` field HF exposes, and split permanent failures by SDK and creation year.

**`BUILD_ERROR` is falling for every SDK — that part looks healthy.** But `RUNTIME_ERROR` diverges sharply for Streamlit in the 2026 cohort:

| SDK | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **streamlit** | 18.1% | **12.4%** | **31.7%** |
| gradio | 47.1% | 27.0% | 20.8% |
| docker | 31.6% | 19.5% | 20.5% |

Gradio and Docker fell or stayed flat over the same period. Streamlit's rate went from 12.4% to 31.7%.

The failure mode also inverted. Among broken Streamlit Spaces created in 2025: 7,991 `BUILD_ERROR` vs 4,582 `RUNTIME_ERROR`. In 2026: **653 `BUILD_ERROR` vs 5,614 `RUNTIME_ERROR`.** Builds started succeeding and apps started crashing instead.

**Checks I ran before posting, because the obvious explanations would each invalidate this:**

- *Bulk uploaders?* No. The top-10 authors account for 2.3% of the 2026 Streamlit cohort, and excluding them entirely moves the rate from 36.6% to 37.1%. It is spread across 12,432 distinct authors.
- *Just young Spaces still settling?* Newer cohorts are consistently *less* broken across every SDK, so a worse young cohort runs against the trend rather than with it. Separately, 300 error-state Spaces re-queried individually with retries were 300/300 still broken with none recovered, so these are not transient.
- *An age artifact?* Age-standardising Streamlit to Gradio's creation-year distribution moves it 43.50% → 41.16%, so the cohort effect here isn't age composition.

**What I can't determine from outside:** whether this is a Streamlit change, a change in the Streamlit runtime image HF builds, or an interaction between the two. HF controls the Space container, so it may not be yours at all — I've filed the general Spaces census with them separately at huggingface/hub-docs#2743.

If it is useful, I can produce the list of affected Space IDs so someone can look at actual tracebacks, which is the thing this analysis can't reach.

Data (1.46M rows, one row per Space): https://huggingface.co/datasets/Ashsinha1/hf-spaces-census
Method and code: https://github.com/ashishsinha1602/dataset-integrity-audit
